An extra vote for either list is worth close to zero for a change-led government, against about 0.7 points per 10,000 votes for Yashar, Together or the Democrats. Rescue voters are about 2% of a station's voters, so use media, digital and calls to identified supporters, not door teams. Launch with the final published polls on Fri 23 Oct. From Sat 24 Oct no rescue message, ad or call script quotes a poll figure: use threshold arithmetic only. Respect both lists, their leaders and reservists' service. See 'Rescue and insurance'.

tactics.effect: Cold texts 0.22 pp per targeted voter in high-salience US races; warm texts to opted-in supporters 0.68 pp [0.05, 1.41]. Danish pooled 0.74 pp, and extra messages to the same person added nothing. In one of the Danish experiments, texts sent before election day beat texts sent on the day.
tactics.israel: Send one or two texts to identified supporters in the 1-3 days before 27 Oct. In a higher-salience US election casual voters responded and habitual voters did not, so aim at supporters who are unsure. The Privacy Protection Authority treats party messages aimed by personal traits as direct mail, by SMS or messaging app. Each must say so, name the database controller and the data source, and offer deletion. Check bulk-messaging and privacy rules with election counsel.

tactics.effect: About 0.74 pp per completed call in high-salience US races. Low-quality vendors about 0.2 pp, high-quality ones 0.9-1.4. A chattier script beat a standard one (3.4 vs 1.2 pp) in a US commercial phone test, and in another test only final-week calls worked. Robocalls have no high-salience estimate.
tactics.israel: Buy only extra capacity for the final week, from a high-quality vendor using a conversational script and the vote-plan questions. Skip robocalls.

tactics.effect: US social-pressure mail gave 1.38 pp in high-salience races. Gratitude mailers gave about 2.4-2.5 pp in lower-salience races, about two-thirds of the effect of the mailer showing a voter's own history. A partisan version of that mailer had no effect.
tactics.israel: Parties cannot be told on election day who has voted. Whether vote-history data may be used before election day is unclear. Send no message that refers to a voter's own past turnout without written clearance from election counsel. Use gentle descriptive norms and thanks, in non-partisan wording, in texts and scripts sent openly in the list's name. No shaming. Check sender-identification and bulk-messaging rules with election counsel.

tactics.effect: Peer-reviewed attitude effects are durable but small (d 0.04-0.08), and argument-only conversations had no effect. The only vote-choice estimate (3.1 net votes per 100 conversations) is a sponsor release. Conversations are long, so each one costs more volunteer time than a standard contact.
tactics.israel: Use trained volunteers with identified soft Netanyahu-bloc voters where the atlas shows persuasion value (default objective): Rishon LeZion and Petah Tikva first (Petah Tikva is the only town where persuasion is the main mechanism), then Holon, Jerusalem and Tel Aviv-Yafo. Listen first. The atlas's persuadable pool, about 87,000 cross-pressured soft Netanyahu-bloc voters or about 2% of voters, is modelled, not measured. It is above the 0.6-1.6% that N12 polls find undecided between blocs, so treat persuasion value as an upper estimate. An Israeli field study found that messages exaggerating hawkish views, without challenging them, made attitudes more conciliatory for up to a year; its vote effect was self-reported. Judge the tactic per volunteer-hour.

tactics.effect: No turnout effect. It protects the count and helps deal with intimidation. Foreign evidence: in Armenia (2003) and Ghana, observers reduced fraud at the stations they covered, and in Ghana some fraud and violence moved to unobserved stations nearby. The research found no Israeli estimate.
tactics.israel: There is one national district, so place people by the votes at stake, not by closeness. The CEC fixed each committee's size and faction mix by 17 Sep. A list with no seat on a committee may send one observer, and counting needs members of at least two factions besides the secretary. Staff every committee seat and observer slot the law allows in stations with large change-bloc vote counts, stations where change lists have no committee member, and stations with past irregularity complaints. Brief them to report disputes and intimidation to election counsel at once. Keep observers on the count, including the central double-envelope tally where the law allows.

tactics.tactic: Election-day festivals and events near polling stations
tactics.effect: US non-partisan festivals raised turnout 6.5 pp at a 50% baseline in low-salience local elections. There is no high-salience or Israeli estimate.
tactics.israel: Activity near polling stations is regulated, and anything of monetary value to voters carries legal risk. Hold no events, food or entertainment near stations; check with election counsel before any election-day presence there.

tactics.effect: No Israeli causal estimate. In the US, a 1 SD longer trip to the polling place (0.245 mile) cut ballots cast by 2-5%.
tactics.israel: The law does not treat driving a voter as a bribe, but election-day transport by outside groups is regulated, and the bloc's own rule is no organised rides. In 2019 the CEC chair held that an NGO's plan to bus voters was politically motivated, and that the group had to register as a body active in the elections. Likud has petitioned against the 2026 expat-flight scheme, alleging bribery and a financing-law breach. Do not organise rides. Help supporters plan the trip with free intercity buses, election-day trains, local transport or a family ride, and check any other transport help with election counsel.

tactics.tactic: Paid persuasion media (online video and digital)
tactics.effect: Small. In 59 US experiments the average ad moved vote choice about 0.7 pp, not significant. In campaigns' own tests, ads routinely differed by about 50% from the average and theory predicted the winners poorly. Effects fade fast: half-lives of about 4 days in a presidential race and 1-2 days in sub-national races. Ads work through persuasion, not turnout.
tactics.israel: Spend in 21-26 Oct, after testing, and put 10-13% of the budget into tests. In US experiments voters were more persuadable about candidates they knew less about. By extension (judgement), information about Eisenkot and Yashar's candidates should move more voters than messages about Netanyahu, whom voters already know well. The rescue and insurance creative runs through this channel too. From Sat 24 Oct no ad quotes a poll figure. Television and radio election broadcasts follow separate election-law rules; check with election counsel before planning any broadcast media. The Messaging page sets out the media plan.

tactics.effect: No rally-specific estimate exists. The closest evidence: across 56 TV debates there was no detectable effect on vote choice. In Italy, candidates canvassing did worse than volunteers.
tactics.israel: The party leader was the main reason for about 19% of voters in 2015 (INES). Use events to recruit volunteers and earn media. Send the right-credentialed leaders (Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman) to persuasion turf, and all leaders to volunteer hubs. Keep visible bloc rallies out of Netanyahu-bloc strongholds, where they can trigger counter-mobilisation.

tactics.tactic: Leaflets, mail, email and digital ads (for turnout)
tactics.effect: Partisan leaflets and mail show no positive effect. GOTV-worded mail gave 0.28 pp per piece in high-salience US races and 0.05 in presidential cycles. Campaign email gave 58.7% turnout against 59.7% in the control group, and purchased Facebook ads showed no effect in two large trials.
tactics.israel: Do not rank turf by the volume of material distributed. Use digital channels to recruit volunteers and relational organisers. Print only a leave-behind with polling-station information.

election_day.title: Chase lagging target stations after each release
election_day.text: The CEC will publish turnout for every regular polling station at least four times during the day, to all lists at once. Before 07:00, give every call-team lead a fixed list of the atlas's positive-value target stations mapped to 2026 station numbers. After each release, rank those stations by how far they trail their locality's turnout in the same release, and move callers and relational reminders to the bottom fifth. Never run area-wide turnout pushes in stations the atlas scores negative or in stations where Arab lists lead. Identified supporters in negative stations outside Arab localities and Arab-led stations, including supporter-list ground such as Netanya, Be'er Sheva and Eilat (default objective) and the negative stations of Jerusalem, are still chased by private calls and texts.

election_day.title: Work from pre-election vote plans
election_day.text: On 17 September the High Court barred party representatives at polling stations from telling their parties which identifiable voters have voted. Callers therefore work from supporters identified before election day. They ask whether the supporter has voted yet and help them plan the trip by public transport or a family ride. Do not organise rides; check any other transport help with election counsel. The ban hurts machines built on individual tracking most, and Likud has said limits on the Elector app force more manual work.

election_day.title: Arab-sector turnout is a leadership decision
election_day.text: The model gives opposite answers under the two objectives. Each 10,000 votes for Ra'am raises the chance of denying Netanyahu 61 seats by about 0.64 points, and each 10,000 for the Joint List by about 0.45. Neither helps a change-led government: Ra'am is close to zero (-0.09) and the Joint List works against it (-0.49). The change bloc runs, funds and brands no turnout work among Arab voters, in Arab localities or in stations where Arab lists lead. Any support leadership approves is independent, transparent and cleared by election counsel in writing, with no operational coordination. Arab parties and civil-society groups run their own campaigns. See the Strategy page.

election_day.title: Blunt Likud's use of the releases
election_day.text: Likud plans to use the station releases to rally its base by pointing to high turnout in change-bloc and Arab areas, echoing its 2015 election-day video. Bank identified change-bloc supporters early through private contact (calls, texts, relational asks), with no public turnout claims. Expect the first releases to show high turnout in our areas, and have the counter-message to our own supporters ready before 10:00: the race is close and every vote counts, without naming any group. Do not publish or celebrate turnout in any area. Rapid-response rules are on the Messaging page.

election_day.title: Get students and young adults home
election_day.text: Voters can vote only at the station of their registered address, and many students and young adults are registered with their parents. Intercity buses on routes over 15 km are free from 20:00 on Mon 26 Oct until service ends on election day. Israel Railways is free on election day (ticket from station counters or machines); confirm Monday-evening trains with the CEC. The announcement does not mention city buses, and Eilat needs advance registration through Egged. Text these supporters the evening before and in the morning with their station address and the last useful bus or train.

election_day.title: Displaced northern and Gaza-border supporters
election_day.text: Between about 40% and 60% of Kiryat Shmona's residents had not returned by September, depending on the report. In the Gaza envelope 90% of evacuees had returned by September 2025, but Be'eri, Nir Oz and Kfar Aza were still largely displaced, some until 2027. In the February 2025 municipal elections, 83 special stations served evacuees from all northern communities; the research found no arrangement yet for the Knesset vote. Confirm the CEC's rules early, then give displaced supporters a trip plan to their station. The atlas halves canvass capacity in these localities. Do not organise rides; check any other travel help with election counsel.

election_day.title: Observers and lawyers in place
election_day.text: There is one national district, so place committee members and observers by the votes at stake: stations with large change-bloc vote counts, stations where change lists have no committee member, and stations with past irregularity complaints. In April 2019 a Likud contractor placed about 1,200 activists with hidden cameras in Arab polling stations, so prepare for intimidation complaints. Keep election counsel on call for station disputes and for questions about transport or activity near polling places. Keep observers on the count, including the central double-envelope tally where the law allows.

dos.title: Identify supporters now, contact them in the final ten days
dos.text: Use 11-16 Oct for supporter ID, list cutting and message tests. In US studies live contact works best in the last 7 to 10 days. In US and UK studies effects add up across contacts with no extra synergy, so put repeat contacts where each one is worth most: identified supporters in positive-value turf who are unsure they will vote. Send texts in the 1-3 days before the vote.

dos.title: Work only turf where turnout nets change votes
dos.text: Extra turnout helps only in proportion to the change bloc's lead among the people mobilised. Walk lists come only from positive-value station areas, never from stations where Arab lists lead. Door value combines turnout and persuasion; rescue runs only through media and calls to identified voters. In supporter-list ground under the default objective (Netanya, Be'er Sheva, Eilat and Beit Shemesh) most of the value is in calls and relational asks to identified supporters, not area canvassing. At 400,000 contacts with 30% of supporters identified, Tel Aviv-Yafo alone yields about 530 of the 1,700 net votes.

dos.title: Test before you spend
dos.text: Ads routinely differ by about 50% in effect, and theory predicts the winners poorly. Run rapid online tests of the main frames this week and put 10-13% of the media budget into testing. Leave a random set of target polling stations unworked so the official results show what the field programme achieved.

dos.title: Use right-credentialed messengers in soft-right turf
dos.text: In a US field experiment, a left-coded group's endorsement acted as a negative cue for right-leaning voters. In Likud-leaning cities and development towns, put Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman, reservists and trusted local figures in front. Reservists speak as civilians only: never on duty, in uniform or with IDF insignia. Parties with a Druze candidate in a winnable slot usually win that candidate's home village, so any Druze work runs through Druze figures on the lists, after a check of the filed CEC lists and a Druze poll. Kamil Abu Rokon has joined Yashar; check his slot on the filed CEC list before naming him in field material. The Golan Druze villages and Ghajar are not targeted.

dos.title: Lead persuasion with competence and unity
dos.text: Campaigns move late deciders by raising the salience of issues they own and by building trust in their leaders. Valence messages beat ideology messages in an Italian field test, and priming cooperation raised tolerance across Israeli party lines. Lead with security record, Oct 7 accountability and equal burden. Keep sharper contrast for mobilising the base. The Messaging page sets out frames, audiences and messengers.

dos.title: Run rescue as insurance media around the final polls
dos.text: Rescue voters are about 2% of a station's voters, so door teams are the wrong channel. Use tested digital and media messages, launched with the final published polls on Fri 23 Oct, plus calls to identified Blue and White supporters from Saturday night after Shabbat to Mon 26 Oct. Call Reservists supporters only if leadership approved it and Friday's polls show the list well below the line. On Friday the ask can point to the final polls and a clear coalition path (see the Coalition page). Friday creative that quotes a poll carries the survey details the law requires, is cleared by election counsel and comes down before the ban starts. From Sat 24 Oct rescue messages and call scripts quote no poll figures and use threshold arithmetic only.

dos.title: Watch allies near the threshold
dos.text: No change list is near the threshold in the forecast: the Democrats pass in 99% of simulations, Yisrael Beytenu in 97% and Together in 99%. Track this daily. If any falls toward the line, each list may run its own insurance messaging for it, but only after both lists' election counsel and treasurers have cleared the spending in writing (Party Financing Law). In 2022 final polls showed Meretz at 4-5 seats, and it fell below the line as votes concentrated on Yesh Atid. See the Strategy page.

dos.title: Split turf by lead change list
dos.text: Assign each polling station (not whole localities) to its lead change list. Where a station's lead list cannot staff it, the locality's lead list (lead_change_list) takes it; if that is the same list, the locality's runner-up (second_change_list) takes it. The four field directors agree the station map, including who covers Tel Aviv-Yafo, by Thu 15 Oct. Each station gets one list's door team, so no household is knocked twice. Lists share only the map and daily aggregate counts. See 'Four lists, one street'.

donts.title: No untargeted turnout work in Netanyahu-bloc strongholds
donts.text: Likud is targeting polling stations where it took about half the vote on about 35% turnout, and values them at 2-3 seats. A joint Likud-RZP programme ranks low-turnout, high-Likud neighbourhoods for door-to-door and phone work. Generic turnout drives there help Likud. Haredi localities turned out at about 75% in 2022, and the atlas projects 91% of their vote to the Netanyahu bloc. The atlas tiers 262 localities as Netanyahu-bloc strongholds. Reach identified supporters and identified soft Netanyahu-bloc voters there by phone only, with no door work, and use door persuasion in Likud-leaning cities. In the scenario engine, 25,000 extra Netanyahu-bloc votes cost about 1.3 points on the chance of a change-led government, nearly as much as 25,000 extra change-list votes add (1.7). See the Strategy page.

donts.title: No change-bloc-run or branded turnout work among Arab voters
donts.text: This covers Arab localities and polling stations where Arab lists lead in mixed cities. Visible campaigns about one group's turnout mobilise the other side. Likud's 2019 camera campaign is widely judged to have helped lift Arab turnout from 49% to 59%, though the Joint List's reunification also contributed and the two effects cannot be separated. Likud plans to use high turnout in change-bloc and Arab areas to rally its base this year. Arab-sector turnout is a leadership decision; any support is independent, transparent and cleared by election counsel.

donts.title: Do not attack the voters you want to win
donts.text: Support for the 2023 judicial overhaul tracked attachment to Netanyahu and hostility to partisan opponents (Israeli panel, 2023), so attacks that raise hostility can harden soft-right voters. In a US field experiment, a group from the other camp acted as a negative cue. Talk to soft Likud voters about competence, repair and fairness, and never mock their 2022 vote.

donts.title: Do not delegitimise Arab voters
donts.text: Most Jewish voters reject a government that relies on Ra'am (57.8% oppose), so in soft-right turf do not build messages around reliance on Ra'am. Lead with competence and a broad government. Never present Arab citizens or their votes as illegitimate. That framing deepens alienation and can depress Arab turnout. The forecast gives the change bloc 61 seats alone in 6.9% of draws, and 26% with Ra'am. See the Coalition page.

donts.title: Do not buy impersonal turnout tools
donts.text: Robocalls, campaign email, purchased social ads and partisan leaflets show turnout effects near zero. Spend that money on volunteer capacity, relational organising and tested persuasion media.

donts.title: Do not run biggest-party appeals against allies
donts.text: Moving votes between Yashar, Together, the Democrats and Yisrael Beytenu adds no bloc seats. In the scenario engine, half a point of the vote moving from Yashar to the Democrats changes the chance of a change-led government by only +0.01 points. Even a new vote for an average change list is worth only about 1/61,000 of an expected bloc seat, because a seat gained by one change list is sometimes taken from another. In 2022 votes concentrated on the largest opposition list and Meretz fell below the threshold. Within-bloc competition matters only for who gets the mandate, and it must stop if an ally nears the threshold. See the Strategy page.

donts.title: Do not disparage Reservists or Blue and White voters
donts.text: Reservists-Economic is a right-of-centre, reservist-branded list. Describe its voters with respect and make the message about threshold arithmetic, not about them. The bloc's equal-burden message depends on reservists: 60% of reservists polled would consider not voting for a party that backs a draft exemption, including 48% of right-wing reservists. Reach reservists as civilians only, never through IDF units, unit chat groups or employers.

donts.title: Do not improvise in legal grey zones
donts.text: The bloc organises no rides and gives voters no gifts or anything of monetary value. Several other things carry legal risk: activity or campaign material near polling stations. So do sharing the voter register or supporter files, bulk texting, publishing or quoting polls during the ban, and messages based on vote history. So do spending by one list that promotes another, and any campaigning through IDF units, bases or employers. The High Court has banned reporting who voted, and the CEC chair treated an NGO's voter-busing plan as election activity. Check with election counsel before any of these.

messages.who_it_moves: Soft-right and traditional Jewish voters, reservist communities, and centre-right voters still split on prime minister (Netanyahu 44%, Eisenkot 21%, Bennett 20%). Security narrowly leads for Jewish voters (39% vs 38% for the economy, top-two shares) and clearly leads on the right (47%).
messages.frame: Competence and record. Show what the change bloc's leaders did in the army and in office, and what they will do next. In US experiments, information about less-known candidates persuaded more. By extension (judgement), the bloc's leaders are a better subject than Netanyahu, whom voters already know well. Security-first framing suits localities hit by the war, where a panel study suggests views have moved right (low confidence) and the vote can still go to Yashar or Together.

messages.issue: Oct 7 accountability and a state commission of inquiry
messages.who_it_moves: Soft Likud voters (Oct 7 was the top reason 2022 Likud voters gave for considering a switch, at 37%), secular young voters (decisive for 22%), and the 40% of Netanyahu-bloc voters who say the failures have not been fixed.
messages.frame: Responsibility and repair. A state commission of inquiry is a majority position (55%), and more voters trust an Eisenkot-led government to fix the failures (48% against 30% for Netanyahu). Frame it as fixing what failed for the voter's family and community. Never blame voters for their 2022 choice.

messages.who_it_moves: Reservists and their families: in a December 2024 poll of reservists, 77% said exemptions are no longer affordable, and 60% would consider not voting for a party that backs one, including 48% of right-wing reservists. Also voters in the centre (34% rank the draft in their top two), secular youth (decisive for 26%), and traditional Shas voters in towns such as Kiryat Shmona, Shlomi and Or Yehuda.
messages.frame: Fairness to those who serve. Equal burden for everyone, said by people who served, speaking as civilians (never in uniform or with IDF insignia). Avoid hostility to haredim as a group. Do not expect it to move national-religious voters, for whom the draft is the top issue for only 15%. This message depends on the reservist constituency, so rescue messaging to Reservists voters must stay respectful.

messages.who_it_moves: Undecided voters (their top concern, at 25%), voters in the centre (the economy is their leading issue, named by 40.5% in their top two, IDI), including Route 4 commuters, and young voters (25%).
messages.frame: Concrete household costs, such as housing, prices and commuting time. Pair it with credibility, since economic attitudes do not line up with Israeli left and right. Its main use is persuasion in Rishon LeZion, Petah Tikva and Holon, and turnout motivation for identified supporters and in positive-value stations, including base towns such as Kfar Saba.

messages.who_it_moves: Undecided voters. In JPPI's August survey undecided Jewish voters emphasised unity and fewer disputes, and in a July Channel 12 poll they named polarisation their second concern (15%) after cost of living (25%). Voters in the centre, whose top issue was unity (30% in JPPI's September index). Soft-right voters wary of the opposition.
messages.frame: A broad government that includes the centre-right. In an Israeli experiment, priming cooperation raised tolerance across party lines, while salient competition raises hostility. Use unity framing in persuasion turf and keep sharper contrast for base mobilisation.

messages.issue: Crime and personal safety in Arab society (context; the Democrats' own outreach only)
messages.who_it_moves: Arab voters open to voting for the Democrats. This is the Democrats' own vote-seeking, not turnout work. Crime is the leading issue: 53.5% name it in their top two (IDI) and about 80% rank it first (Statnet). More than 140 people were killed in Arab communities by late June 2026.
messages.frame: Concrete plans on policing, crime and personal safety. The change bloc does not script messages for Arab lists or civil-society groups and runs no turnout messaging among Arab voters. The Democrats, who are touring Arab towns for votes, can carry this frame in their own campaign, transparently and within counsel's rules. While Ra'am sits near the threshold, this outreach should not aim at Ra'am's voters (see the Strategy page).

messages.issue: Northern rebuilding and fair treatment of the periphery
messages.who_it_moves: Northern Jewish towns such as Kiryat Shmona, Nahariya, Karmiel, Ma'alot, Tiberias and Shlomi. Across the Haifa and Northern districts (Midgam, April 2026), 65% say the state is abandoning the north, and opposition parties lead 38% to 26% with 27% undecided. Druze towns with planning and Nation-State Law grievances.
messages.frame: Local and practical. Talk about services, rebuilding and jobs, through trusted local figures. Kiryat Shmona's Likud share fell from 58% in 2020 to 49% in 2022, and the Likud-backed mayoral candidate came second in the first round in 2025. In Druze towns the same frame means planning and zoning relief and equality under the Nation-State Law, using only commitments in the lists' published platforms or cleared by list leadership, and carried by Druze figures on the lists. In Likud-leaning Jewish towns these are persuasion messages, because generic turnout work there helps Likud. Druze towns are held out until a check of the filed CEC lists and a Druze poll, because their 2026 vote depends on which lists placed Druze candidates in winnable slots.

messages.who_it_moves: Supporters of Blue and White (forecast about 0.6%) and Reservists (forecast about 1.7%), about 100,000 voters at regular polling stations in the atlas, plus voters weighing other small lists.
messages.frame: Make your vote count toward the government you want. In 2022 about 289,000 votes for Meretz and Balad fell below the threshold, Meretz missed by 4,061 votes, and the Netanyahu bloc won 64 seats from a near-tie in votes. On Fri 23 Oct the ask can point to the final published polls and a clear coalition path. Friday creative that quotes a poll carries the survey details the law requires, is cleared by election counsel and comes down before the ban starts. From Sat 24 Oct it uses threshold arithmetic only and quotes no poll figure. Respect the list, its leader and reservists' service; the message is about the arithmetic, not the voters.

sections.title: What a realistic field programme buys
sections.text: The atlas's planner spends a fixed budget of completed contacts on the best positive-value turf. It leaves out Arab localities, polling stations where Arab lists lead (in mixed cities, Jerusalem and mixed Druze towns), the access-excluded villages and, until a candidate check and a Druze poll, Druze towns. It sends door teams only where at least 1,000 contacts are available. Two budgets bracket a realistic programme, 150,000 and 400,000 completed contacts, each run with no supporter lists and with 30% of supporters identified. On those numbers field work is a margin lever worth roughly 760 to 2,100 net votes, depending on budget and objective. The atlas's baselines are a change-led government in 22% of draws, the Netanyahu bloc held below 61 in 87%, and about 51 expected change-bloc seats. Since the 13 Oct update the forecast carries the same six surplus pairs, so these match its headline closely: the formation model gives a change-led government 22%, and the Netanyahu bloc reaches 61 in 13% of draws.
bullets: Change-led government: 150,000 contacts buy about 760 net votes with no supporter lists and about 1,000 with 30% identified. 400,000 contacts buy about 1,400 and 1,700. That is +0.05 to +0.12 points on the chance of a change-led government. Ranges across the atlas's assumption sets: about 420-1,500, 640-2,100, 770-3,200 and 1,100-4,300.
Deny Netanyahu 61: about 930 and 1,000 net votes at 150,000 contacts, and about 1,600 and 1,800 at 400,000 (+0.04 to +0.08 points). Ranges: about 510-1,600, 580-2,100, 920-3,500 and 1,000-4,300.

Change-bloc seats: about 840 and 1,300 net votes at 150,000 contacts, and about 1,600 and 2,100 at 400,000, or about 0.015 to 0.037 expected seats. Ranges: about 460-1,500, 910-2,200, 890-3,400 and 1,400-4,300. One net vote for an average change list is worth about 1/61,000 of an expected seat.

Compare the national levers on the Strategy page. The scenario engine sizes each lever if it happens, not how likely it is. Half a point of the vote moving from Likud to the change lists is worth about +3.1 points on the chance of a change-led government, 25,000 extra change-list votes about +1.7, and a Blue and White withdrawal with endorsement about +1.7. A realistic field programme is worth about +0.1. Field work protects margins. It does not replace those levers.

Treat the totals as orders of magnitude. The turnout effect drives most of the spread: the low end of each range assumes an effect about half as large, and the high end drops the turnout hump (for change-bloc seats at 150,000 contacts with lists, tripling the rescue effect sets the high end). Rankings of places are steadier than totals: 16 localities stay in the change-led-government top 25 in every sensitivity scenario.

Druze towns are held out of these totals until a check of the filed CEC lists and a Druze poll, because their 2026 vote depends on which lists placed Druze candidates in winnable slots. If cleared, they would add about 140 to 200 net votes for a change-led government, about 270 to 320 under deny-61 and about 160 to 210 for change-bloc seats, depending on the plan.

Saturation, meaning every positive station area at 35% of the roll plus list programmes at 30% identified, is a model ceiling of about 3,200 net votes for a change-led government across all localities, or about 2,800 outside Arab localities and the held-out Druze towns. It needs about 1.3 million contacts, about 1.1 million of them door conversations. Treat it as a ceiling, not a plan.

Supporter lists pay only if they exist. At the same contact budget, list calls to identified voters (supporters, soft Netanyahu-bloc voters and Blue and White or Reservists voters) add about 240 net votes at 150,000 contacts and about 370 at 400,000 (change-led government). They carry much of the value in Jerusalem, Netanya, Ashdod and Bat Yam, and bring in Be'er Sheva, Eilat, Ashkelon and Hadera through calls alone. The 400,000-contact plan assumes files on about 120,000 change supporters already exist. The ID contacts needed to build them are not counted, so first ask how many identified supporters the four lists already hold in these towns.
Value is concentrated. At 400,000 contacts with 30% identified, Tel Aviv-Yafo yields about 530 net votes, Haifa 130, Ramat Gan 86, Jerusalem 73, Rishon LeZion 66, Herzliya 61 and Netanya 60.

Kibbutzim and moshavim fall below the 1,000-contact door minimum, so the planner sends no door teams there and most are tiered low yield. Reach supporters there through members' own community networks and texts to identified supporters. That work is not in these totals.

Why it still matters: in 2022 the Netanyahu bloc finished about 30,000 votes ahead, Meretz missed the threshold by 4,061 votes, and in April 2019 New Right missed it by 1,453. Ra'am passes in about 80% of simulations and RZP-Zehut in about 52%. Threshold races are decided by margins of this size.

What the numbers leave out: polling-committee and observer coverage, paid media, the rescue media programme and relational work in small communities. The effect sizes are borrowed from foreign experiments. European canvassing effects are well below US ones, and no Israeli randomised turnout trial exists.

sections.title: Four lists, one street
sections.text: Yashar, Together, the Democrats and Yisrael Beytenu will canvass the same streets. Moving a vote from one change list to another adds no bloc seats: in the scenario engine, half a point of the vote moving from Yashar to the Democrats changes the chance of a change-led government by +0.01 points. A household knocked by two lists is a duplicated contact. Split turf, share counts and keep the doorstep positive. See the Strategy page.
bullets: Split turf at polling-station level, not locality level. The atlas gives each station its lead change list (lead_change_list) and each locality a runner-up (second_change_list). Even at station level, outside Arab localities, Arab-led stations and the held-out Druze towns, Yashar leads about 4,800 of the roughly 5,800 positive-value stations under the default objective, the Democrats about 540, Yisrael Beytenu about 470 and Together 7. So staffing decides the rest. Where a station's lead list cannot staff it, the locality's lead list (lead_change_list) takes it; if that is the same list, the locality's runner-up (second_change_list) takes it.

The four field directors agree the station map by Thu 15 Oct. Settle Tel Aviv-Yafo first: it is the largest single prize (about 530 net votes in the 400,000-contact plan with lists), Yashar leads about 360 of its positive stations and the Democrats about 240, and Yashar's own campaign has avoided Tel Aviv.

Yashar leads in most large target localities, with Together the runner-up across much of the Sharon and Gush Dan and the Democrats runner-up in Tel Aviv-Yafo, Jerusalem and Givatayim. Yisrael Beytenu leads in places such as Akko, Nof HaGalil, Qiryat Yam, Arad and Ari'el.

Respect existing splits where they fit the atlas. Yashar is working soft-Likud voters (a pool of about 200,000) and runs a religious-Zionist headquarters covering Gush Etzion, Efrat, Givat Shmuel and Ariel. Yisrael Beytenu has mapped Likud's best stations, including Russian-speaking ex-Likud voters. Yashar launched as a campaign for the Route 4 suburbs.

Share only aggregates and station maps between lists: the turf map, station assignments and daily counts (doors knocked, supporters identified, vote plans made). Share no voter-level records between lists unless election counsel has cleared the format in writing. Parties may receive the voter register but may not pass it to third parties.

Each list pays for its own field work. Staff time, volunteers' paid costs, call centres or media that one list funds to promote another need prior written clearance from both lists' election counsel and treasurers (Party Financing Law).

No list attacks another list's voters on the doorstep. Partisan contact can demobilise a rival's supporters, and in 2022 votes concentrated on Yesh Atid while Meretz fell below the threshold. Keep within-bloc competition, such as Together's bid to win back ex-Yesh Atid voters from Yashar, to paid media and leaders' messages.

If any ally falls toward the threshold, each list may run its own insurance messaging for it, but only after both lists' election counsel and treasurers have cleared the spending in writing (Party Financing Law).

Druze towns wait for a check of the filed CEC lists and a Druze poll. Any work there then goes to whichever list placed a Druze candidate in a winnable slot, led by that candidate's local figures. The Golan Druze villages and Ghajar are not targeted.
Set a minimum deployment. Door teams go only where at least 1,000 contacts are available; group small targets into one team-day instead of splitting them between lists.

sections.title: Rescue and insurance: a media programme
sections.text: Rescue means persuading supporters of lists likely to miss the 3.25% threshold to vote for a list that will pass. The main target is Blue and White (forecast about 0.6%, pass chance 1%). Reservists-Economic (forecast about 1.7%, pass chance 21%) is a target only if leadership approves it by Thu 15 Oct and Friday's final polls show the list well below the line. Otherwise treat it as a possible partner (see the Coalition page). Rescue voters are about 2% of a typical station's voters, so door canvassing is the wrong channel, and the atlas counts no rescue at the door. Run rescue as media, digital and insurance messaging launched with the final published polls on Fri 23 Oct, plus calls to identified voters from Saturday night after Shabbat to Mon 26 Oct.
bullets: Channels: tested digital and media creative, and calls and relational asks to identified Blue and White and Reservists supporters. No door teams.

Timing: build call lists during supporter ID from 11 Oct and creative from 17 Oct, ready by Thu 22 Oct. Launch digital and media messages as the final polls are published on Fri 23 Oct. Run calls to identified voters from Saturday night after Shabbat through Mon 26 Oct, using threshold arithmetic and no poll figures.

Poll ban: from Sat 24 Oct no rescue message, ad or call script quotes any poll figure. Use threshold arithmetic only: a list under 3.25% elects no one, and in 2022 Meretz missed by 4,061 votes. Friday creative that quotes a poll runs only in digital placements with an end time scheduled at launch, before the ban starts; it carries the survey details the law requires and is cleared by election counsel in advance. Print, outdoor and broadcast creative quotes no poll figures. Delete organic posts that quote polls before the ban, or get counsel's ruling that they may stay up. Quoting or re-publishing any poll result during the ban needs a written ruling from election counsel.

Forecast and polls differ. The 0.6% and 1.7% are forecast shares. Blue and White is below the threshold in every published poll since mid-September that lists it (0.3-2.0%), but about half of published polls since mid-September (19 of 34 to 12 Oct) show the Reservists at 4-5 seats, including Kan on 11 Oct and Channel 12 and Channel 14 on 12 Oct. Others, including i24 and most Channel 13 and Channel 14 polls, put them below the line. Rescue messaging to Reservists voters works only if Friday's final polls show them below the line.

Why the final polls matter: voters desert lists they expect to fall short, and the final polls feed that expectation. In 2015 Yachad polled 4-5 seats in the final polls and won none; in 2022 Jewish Home polled 1.5-2.2% and won 1.19%. Final polls are also a poor guide near the line. Since 2009, lists averaging 3.5-4.5 seats over the final three weeks failed 2 times in 9, and lists averaging 0.5-3.5 seats passed 5 times in 9. The samples are small.

Size: the atlas counts only the calls, and assumes, without experimental support, that 5% of contacted voters move, 60% to change lists and 40% to Likud. At saturation the calls are worth about 190 net votes for a change-led government and about 480 for change-bloc seats. The media programme is not in the model.

Trade-off: under the deny-61 objective, rescue calls to Reservists voters do not help in the model. A vote that stays with the Reservists counts against a Netanyahu 61 if the list passes (pass chance about 21%), and 40% of movers are assumed to go to Likud. Under deny-61 the calls are worth close to nothing (about 40 net votes at saturation). Leadership decides whether to target Reservists voters at all. Blue and White voters are the cleaner target.

Withdrawal scenarios point the same way. If the Reservists withdrew and 60% of their voters moved to change lists, the scenario engine gives about +1.6 points on the chance of a change-led government but -0.8 points on deny-61. If most moved right (65% to Likud and Otzma), both fall (-1.0 and -3.0 points). These are sizes if it happens, not forecasts. See the Strategy page.

Reservists framing: it is a right-of-centre, reservist-branded list. Use reservists as messengers, as civilians only (never on duty, in uniform or with IDF insignia), respect their service and talk about threshold arithmetic. The bloc's equal-burden message depends on this constituency: 60% of reservists polled would consider not voting for a party that backs a draft exemption, including 48% of right-wing reservists. Its leader, Yoaz Hendel, says he will not complete a majority with haredi parties or be the 61st seat of a government that depends on Arab parties, and that Netanyahu should go (see the Coalition page).

Blue and White: on 10 Oct Gantz said he is 'running until the end'. On 20 Sep he had said he would halt his campaign if final-week polls showed the list below the threshold, and senior opposition figures have pressed him to quit. The forecast now models withdrawal at 0.25. The research found no explicit rule on a list withdrawing after approval. Ballots are printed for the lists published on Sun 18 Oct, so a later exit could leave its slips in the booth and votes cast for it would be wasted. Election counsel should confirm. If Gantz withdraws and endorses, and his voters split as the model assumes (60% Yashar, 25% Together, 15% abstain), the scenario engine adds about 1.7 points to the chance of a change-led government and about 0.9 to deny-61. Voters of withdrawn lists tend to follow their own views, not the leader's deal, so the real gain depends on where they go. If it happens, offer its voters a respectful next step. See the Strategy page.

Allies come first. If the Democrats, Yisrael Beytenu or Together slips toward the threshold, each list may run its own insurance messaging for it, but only after both lists' election counsel and treasurers have cleared the spending in writing (Party Financing Law).

sections.title: Young voters, students and soldiers
sections.text: First-time and young voters are numerous, less certain to vote and often not living where they are registered. Every contact with them starts with the registered address.
bullets: Registration address: voters may vote only at the station of their registered address, which is fixed by a Population Registry cut-off well before the vote (54 days before in 2022). Many students and young adults are registered with their parents, so build each one a trip plan to that station.

Travel: intercity buses on routes over 15 km are free from 20:00 on Mon 26 Oct until service ends on election day. Israel Railways is free on election day (ticket from station counters or machines); confirm Monday-evening trains with the CEC. The announcement does not mention city buses, and Eilat needs advance registration through Egged. Election day is a statutory holiday.

Size and lean: estimates run from about 550,000 (Midgam) to about 640,000 (CBS, via IDI) first-time voters. Among Jewish first-time voters Midgam found Yashar 16%, Likud 14%, Together 10%, the Democrats 7%, Yisrael Beytenu 6% and 10% undecided, and 74% place themselves right or centre-right.

Certainty: in a Dialog poll of 18-22-year-olds, 67% were certain to vote, and 14% were undecided on party (20% of young women, 8% of young men). Draft policy was decisive for 26% of secular youth and the Oct 7 inquiry for 22%.
Campuses: recruit volunteers and relational organisers, run vote-plan conversations and record where each student is registered. Friend-to-friend texting had large turnout effects in a US trial.
Families: in Danish experiments, a text to a young voter reached housemates (about 30% spillover) but not parents living elsewhere, so contact parents separately.

Soldiers: soldiers away from home vote by double envelope, the largest group of envelope voters, and their ballots are counted centrally after the regular count. Reach soldiers and reservists as civilians only, through family and friends: never through IDF units, unit chat groups, bases, uniforms or insignia, and never through employers. Check with election counsel.
Why it lasts: in US studies, voting once raised the chance of voting in a later election by about 10 points, and the forecast gives a repeat election a 47% chance (see the Coalition page).

sections.title: The Arab-sector decision for leadership
sections.text: Whether the change bloc puts any resources into Arab-sector turnout is a leadership decision, not a field-team one. The model gives opposite answers under the two objectives. Whatever leadership decides, the change bloc runs, funds and brands no turnout work among Arab voters, in Arab localities or in stations where Arab lists lead, and any support is independent, transparent and cleared by election counsel.
bullets: The trade-off: per 10,000 extra votes, Ra'am adds -0.09 points and the Joint List -0.49 points to the chance of a change-led government, but +0.64 and +0.45 points to the chance of denying Netanyahu 61. In the formation model these votes turn Netanyahu-bloc wins into deadlock while diluting change-list seats. The atlas's seat law carries all six surplus pairs, including Joint List-Ra'am and Together-Yisrael Beytenu.

At national scale, in the scenario engine, Arab turnout 5 points higher (about 46,000 votes for the Joint List and Ra'am) lowers the chance of a change-led government by about 1.4 points and raises the chance of denying Netanyahu 61 by about 2.1 points. That is context for leadership, not a field target. See the Strategy page.

Under the change-led-government objective the model recommends no investment. Under deny-61 the value lies in Arab voters' own lists, and the atlas makes no field recommendation on where or among whom. That is for leadership, through election counsel.

Context: the change bloc reaches 61 seats alone in 6.9% of forecast draws and in 26% with Ra'am. The Netanyahu bloc reaches 61 in 13%, so it is held below 61 in 87%. The formation model gives a change coalition with Ra'am 7.5% and a repeat election 47%. See the Coalition page.

Rules: no change-bloc-run, funded or branded turnout work among Arab voters, and no operational coordination with Arab parties or civil-society groups. The change bloc names no messengers and writes no scripts for Arab-sector turnout work. In 2019 the CEC chair held that an NGO's plan to bus about 15,000 voters was politically motivated and required the group to register as a body active in the elections. Coordination with a party could raise party-financing questions as well. Any support leadership approves needs written clearance from election counsel.

Why branding backfires: Likud's 2019 camera campaign is widely judged to have helped lift Arab turnout from 49% to 59%, though the Joint List's reunification also contributed. Likud plans to use the station turnout releases to point to high turnout in change-bloc and Arab areas.

Arab lists are independent and are not members of the bloc. The Democrats' own campaign for Arab votes, including tours of Arab towns and Arabic social media, is that list's decision under the same transparent, counsel-cleared rules.

For leadership's information: Arab turnout was 53.2% in 2022, and scenario polling links the configuration now running (a three-party Joint List and a separate Ra'am) to about 59%. Crime is the leading issue. Rhetoric that paints reliance on Arab parties as illegitimate can depress turnout.

Language and the atlas: never call Arab or Druze towns change-majority, and never describe Arab towns as change-bloc turf. The atlas tiers Arab localities as Arab-list turf under every objective and publishes no town-level targeting values or ranks for them, only segment totals. The planner never includes Arab localities or polling stations where Arab lists lead in mixed cities, Jerusalem or mixed Druze towns.

sections.title: Legal guardrails
sections.text: Election-day transport, gifts, campaign activity near polling stations and the publication of polls are regulated under Israeli election law. The points below are what the research found; they are not legal advice. For anything else, check with election counsel before acting, and keep a written log of clearances.
bullets: Who has voted: on 17 Sep 2026 the High Court barred party representatives at polling stations from telling their parties which identifiable voters have voted, citing election law and privacy law. Parties may still urge people to vote.
Station turnout: the CEC will publish aggregate turnout for every regular station at least four times on election day, to all lists at once and with no names.

Voter data and supporter files: parties receive the voter register but may not pass it to third parties. Between lists, share only aggregates and station maps unless election counsel clears a voter-level format in writing; the same applies to outside groups and vendors. Whether vote-history data may be used before election day is unclear, so send no message that refers to a voter's own past turnout without clearance.

Cross-list activity: staff time, volunteers' paid costs, call centres or media that one list funds to promote another list need prior written clearance from both lists' election counsel and treasurers (Party Financing Law: spending by a body linked to a party counts as that party's spending).

Transport: the law says driving a voter to and from the polling station is not a bribe, but outside groups that spend more than NIS 120,400 on election activity, including election-day transport, must register with the State Comptroller. In 2019 the CEC chair held that an NGO's plan to bus voters was politically motivated and that the group had to register as a body active in the elections. Likud has challenged the 2026 expat-flight scheme as bribery and a financing breach. The bloc's own rule is no organised rides. Help with public transport or a family ride only, and check any other transport help with election counsel.

Gifts and benefits: the bloc gives voters no gifts, food, entertainment, travel or other benefits. Election propaganda may not be tied to gifts or entertainment, and food may accompany it only at parties in private homes. Offering any service or benefit in return for a vote is bribery, punishable by up to 5 years. Clear any house-meeting catering with election counsel.

Near polling stations: campaign propaganda of any kind is an offence inside a polling place or within 5 metres of its gate (10 metres from the walls where there is no fence). Rallies, processions, loudspeakers and radio or TV propaganda are banned from 19:00 on Mon 26 Oct. Hold no events and serve no food near stations. Clear any other presence or material near stations with counsel, and brief committee members and observers on their role.

Polls: final polls may be published until the end of Fri 23 Oct. A published poll must state who commissioned and conducted it, the fieldwork dates, the population sampled, how many were approached and took part, and the margin of error. Print and online publishers must also give the questions. From Sat 24 Oct to the close of polls, publish, post or leak no poll, including internal ones. Confirm the exact cut-off with counsel.

Poll figures in campaign material: from Sat 24 Oct no rescue message, ad or call script quotes any poll figure; use threshold arithmetic only. Quoting or re-publishing any poll result in campaign material, ads or scripted calls during the ban needs a written ruling from election counsel.

Soldiers and reservists: reach them as civilians only. Never campaign through IDF units, unit chat groups or bases, never use uniforms or insignia, and never recruit or message through employers. In 2026 the CEC chair, on Likud petitions, ordered Yashar to remove a video with AI-generated soldiers and Bennett to cut IDF segments from a Together video.
Outside groups: joint activity with an NGO or civil-society group may raise election-activity and party-financing questions. Clear it with counsel first.

Bulk messaging and privacy: the Privacy Protection Authority treats party messages aimed by personal traits as direct mail on any channel. Each must say so, name the database controller and the data source, and offer deletion. A missing notice can cost NIS 50-100 per person contacted, and enforcement paused during the campaign can follow after the vote. WhatsApp bans accounts that show bulk or automated behaviour. Check the rules with counsel before the final-week waves.

sources.citation: The Knesset Model (2026, 13 Oct). Wasted votes by list, 2019-2022, and expected waste in 2026. Calculation from the Central Elections Committee's official locality results (21st-25th Knesset) and the forecast's published 13 October simulations.
sources.checked: corrected: the official figures reproduce exactly. Re-run on the published 13 October simulations: expected waste about 8%, between 4% and 12% in most simulations. The Netanyahu bloc's 3.5 points come from RZP (1.0), The Haredi Public (0.8), Amcha (0.7), Otzma (0.5) and Noam (0.5). Other micro-lists add 2.7 points and Blue and White plus Reservists-Economic 1.2. An earlier 19-list build gave about 5%.
sources.note: Votes for lists below the threshold ran from under 1% (2020) to almost 9% (April 2019 and 2022), each time hurting mainly one camp. In the published 13 October simulations about 8% of the vote is expected to be wasted. The largest share, about 3.5 points, is on the Netanyahu side. Micro-lists outside both blocs add about 2.7 points, Blue and White and Reservists-Economic about 1.2, the Arab lists 0.5 and the change lists 0.1.

sources.citation: The Knesset Model (2026). Seat-formula counterfactuals for the 25th Knesset (2022). Recount of the Central Elections Committee's official results with the actual surplus-vote agreements.
sources.checked: corrected: if Balad had also passed, its new votes would have raised the threshold, so Meretz would have needed about 4,600 votes from Yesh Atid, not 4,062, for the bloc to fall to 60. A Labor-Meretz merger keeping about 55% or more of their votes would have cut the bloc to 62-63 seats. The Netanyahu bloc's agreements together were worth one seat, and either Likud-RZP or Shas-UTJ alone would have secured it.
sources.note: The recount reproduces the 2022 seats exactly. Had Meretz gained the roughly 4,060 votes it lacked, taken from Yesh Atid, Netanyahu's bloc would have won 62 seats, not 64.

sources.citation: The Knesset Model (2026). Seat-formula counterfactual for the April 2019 election. Recount of the Central Elections Committee's official results (21st Knesset), with the surplus agreements reported by the Jewish Virtual Library and Israel Hayom.
sources.checked: corrected: New Right was 1,454 votes short, not 1,455. Under the agreements actually reported (Likud-URWP, New Right-Yisrael Beytenu, Shas-UTJ, Labor-Meretz and the Arab pair), a New Right pass gives Netanyahu's bloc without Yisrael Beytenu 62 seats. Across all 3,600 agreement structures consistent with the result the range is 60-64, and 61-63 in 98.5% of them. The link to the September repeat election is an inference.
sources.note: New Right missed the April 2019 threshold by about 1,450 votes. Had it passed, Netanyahu's bloc without Liberman would most likely have had 62 seats rather than 60.

sources.citation: Wikipedia contributors (accessed 2026). 1992 Israeli legislative election (official results table). Wikipedia. Also: Israel Democracy Institute (n.d.). 1992 elections. Seat recount by The Knesset Model.
sources.checked: corrected: 1992 did have surplus agreements (Likud-Tzomet and Tehiya-Moledet). With them, a 1% threshold would have given Tehiya a seat at the Arab Democratic Party's expense and tied the blocs 60-60, so 'still 61-59' holds only with no agreements. The Tehiya-to-Likud result (60-60) holds either way.
sources.note: Right-wing lists below the new 1.5% threshold wasted about 48,500 votes in 1992. Had Tehiya's votes gone to Likud, the blocs would have tied 60-60 and Rabin would have had no blocking majority.

sources.citation: Bochsler, D. (2010). Who gains from apparentments under D'Hondt? Electoral Studies 29(4): 617-627. Also: Janson, S. (2014). Asymptotic bias of some election methods. Annals of Operations Research 215(1): 89-136 (doi:10.1007/s10479-012-1141-2). Schuster, K., Pukelsheim, F., Drton, M., & Draper, N. R. (2003). Seat biases of apportionment methods for proportional representation. Electoral Studies 22(4): 651-676.
sources.checked: corrected: Janson does not cite Bochsler. The rule that a pair gains about half a seat times one minus its combined share is Janson's theorem, not a new model result. The model adds the chance that both partners pass and confirms the rule. Schuster et al.'s seat biases (+5/12, -1/12 and -4/12 of a seat) are for parties ranked by size with random vote shares.
sources.note: Theory for seat formulas like Israel's: a surplus-vote agreement never costs seats and is worth at most about half a seat. It is worth less as the pair's combined size grows, and nothing if either partner fails.

sources.citation: The Knesset Model (2026, 13 Oct). Scenario runs on the forecast's published 13 October simulations (8,000 outcomes, 21-list fit) through the seat law: surplus-agreement values, Blue and White withdrawal, Reservists-Economic passing or collapsing, and threshold outcomes by list (internal).
sources.checked: corrected: re-run on the published 13 October simulations. The Blue and White and Reservists collapse scenarios depend on how the change-camp share is split among the change lists, which moves results by about 0.1 point. In the Blue and White scenarios most of the gain goes to Yashar and Together, while the Democrats and Yisrael Beytenu lose a few hundredths of a seat. The model's published exchange rate for 10,000 extra Reservists votes is -0.01 points for a change-led government and +0.16 points for denying Netanyahu 61, not +0.03 and +0.2.
sources.note: The two change-bloc surplus agreements add about 0.6 expected seats together and cut the chance of a Netanyahu majority by about 1.5 points. A Blue and White withdrawal moves that chance by under a point, depending on how many of its voters go to Likud. Reservists-Economic passing lowers it but also cuts the change bloc's own seats. Netanyahu's bloc reaches 61 far more often in simulations where RZP, Otzma or Amcha pass, a correlation rather than a cause.

sources.citation: The Knesset Model (2026). How much of their components' combined share Israeli joint lists kept, 2009-2022. Calculation from official Central Elections Committee results and Israel Democracy Institute election pages.
sources.checked: corrected: the count depends on which cases are included. Adding the 2013 Jewish Home-Tkuma union (+47% on its components) gives two of seven Jewish-sector unions that beat the sum of their parts, not one of six. The model's 0.75 merger-retention assumption inherits this choice of cases.
sources.note: Most Jewish-sector mergers since 2013 kept only 64-85% of their components' combined share. Arab reunifications gained: the Joint List rose 15% in 2015 and 36% in September 2019.

sources.citation: Gschwend, T., & Hooghe, M. (2008). Should I stay or should I go? An experimental study on voter responses to pre-electoral coalitions. European Journal of Political Research 47(5): 556-577.
sources.checked: corrected: the experiment was run with first-year students in three academic years (2003-2005), using the 2004 regional ballot. It was not run during the 2004 campaign itself.
sources.note: Belgian ballot experiment with 1,255 students: 89% of senior-partner supporters stayed with a joint list, against 77% of junior-partner supporters. Desertion rose with dislike of the partner and ideological distance. Foreign evidence from a student sample.

sources.citation: Hortala-Vallve, R., Meriläinen, J., & Tukiainen, J. (2021). Pre-Electoral Coalitions: Insights into the Boundaries of Political Parties. APSA Preprints (working paper).
sources.checked: corrected: the penalty of about one point of vote share (about 6% of a party's share) is the average across all joint lists. For ideologically close partners the estimate is smaller and not significant. These are Finnish municipal alliances in which parties keep their own labels and candidates, so the result gives a direction, not a number to plan with.
sources.note: Finnish municipal elections: parties in ideologically mixed joint lists lost vote share, while close partners showed no significant penalty. Foreign evidence from an unpublished paper.

sources.citation: Golder, S. N. (2006). Pre-electoral coalition formation in parliamentary democracies. British Journal of Political Science 36(2): 193-212. Also: Golder, S. N. (2005). Pre-electoral coalitions in comparative perspective: a test of existing hypotheses. Electoral Studies 24(4): 643-663. Debus, M. (2009). Pre-electoral commitments and government formation. Public Choice 138(1-2): 45-64.
sources.checked: corrected: Debus's abstract has now been checked and confirms that pre-electoral commitments, both pacts and rejections, significantly affect which governments form. The change bloc has two surplus agreements, not three. Together's merger fits threshold pressure on Yesh Atid but not Golder's finding that partners of similar size combine most often.
sources.note: In 20 parliamentary democracies (1946-1998), pre-electoral coalitions form most often between ideologically compatible parties of similar size, under disproportional rules and polarisation. Pre-election commitments then shape which government forms.

sources.citation: Times of Israel staff (2022, 12 Sep). Labor leader Michaeli rejects Lapid's incentives for union between her party, Meretz. The Times of Israel. Also: Times of Israel staff (2022, 3 Nov). Meretz wiped out of the Knesset after falling just below electoral threshold.
sources.checked: verified. The final official count has Meretz 4,061 votes short (150,793 votes, 3.16%), not the 3,800 reported on election night.
sources.note: In 2022 Labor refused a merger with Meretz despite Lapid's offers. Meretz then missed the threshold, and its leader blamed Yesh Atid for draining its allies.

sources.citation: Times of Israel staff (2019, 29 Aug). Zehut bows out of elections after Netanyahu promises Feiglin a cabinet post. The Times of Israel. Also: JNS (2019). Zehut members vote 3 to 1 to accept Likud deal.
sources.checked: corrected: 29 August (day 19) was the announcement. Members approved the deal by about 3 to 1 on 1 September (day 16), and Zehut then withdrew. The approval is confirmed by JNS, not by the Times of Israel article.
sources.note: Zehut withdrew from the September 2019 election 16 days before the vote and was absent from the official results. Its voters did not follow it to Likud.

sources.citation: The Knesset Model (2026). Backtest of final Israeli polls against results for lists near the threshold, 2009-2022. Polls compiled from Wikipedia's Israeli opinion-polling pages and compared with official results.
sources.checked: corrected: the backtest reproduces. Blue and White's February 2021 polling was about 3-3.3 seats with 21-29% of polls at zero, all of those from one pollster. It was not 2.9 seats with a third at zero.
sources.note: Final polls mis-call lists near the threshold in both directions. Lists averaging 0.5-3.5 seats failed 44% of the time and lists at 3.5-4.5 seats 22% of the time. Meretz (2022) never polled below 4 seats and failed, while Ra'am (2021) averaged 1.7 and won 4.

sources.citation: Wikipedia contributors (accessed 2026). United Arab List. Wikipedia. With official Central Elections Committee results, Ynetnews on the Ra'am-Joint List surplus agreement, and the forecast's 13 October simulations.
sources.checked: corrected: in the published 13 October simulations Ra'am passes in about 80%, and Netanyahu's bloc reaches 61 in about 10% of those against about 27% where Ra'am fails. That gap is a correlation, since a Ra'am failure coincides with low Arab turnout. The signed Ra'am-Joint List agreement is sourced to Ynetnews, which shows no date.
sources.note: Ra'am has finished just above the threshold in each of its last three runs (3.3-4.1%). It was disqualified on 23 September 2026 and restored by the Supreme Court on 2 October. In the 13 October simulations, Netanyahu's bloc reaches 61 in about 10% of outcomes where Ra'am passes and about 27% where it fails.

sources.citation: Fredén, A. (2014). Threshold insurance voting in PR systems: A study of voters' strategic behavior in the 2010 Swedish General Election. Journal of Elections, Public Opinion and Parties 24(4): 473-492.
sources.checked: verified. The paper is paywalled. The detail that most Christian Democrat voters preferred the Moderates comes from the author's own published summary.
sources.note: Sweden 2010: some voters backed an at-risk junior partner (the Christian Democrats) to keep their preferred government viable. Foreign evidence with no effect size.

sources.citation: Meffert, M. F., & Gschwend, T. (2011). Polls, coalition signals and strategic voting: An experimental investigation of perceptions and effects. European Journal of Political Research 50(5): 636-667.
sources.checked: corrected: the published article does not find a strong effect of coalition signals. Only 5% of participants cast explicitly strategic votes, against 24% insincere votes. Neither the manipulated poll nor the manipulated signal changed votes directly. Believing one's party had no chance raised defection by up to 40 points, and noticing a signal by up to 8 points (weakly significant).
sources.note: German experiment run during two 2006 state campaigns: strategic voting in the strict sense is a minority behaviour, and what voters believe about a party's chances matters more than the cues themselves.

sources.citation: Wikipedia contributors (accessed 2026). 2013 Lower Saxony state election (official results table). Wikipedia.
sources.checked: corrected: the source shows the sequence (the FDP polled about 4.5-5%, won 9.9%, and the CDU lost power by one seat), not the counterfactual. Reading it as loan votes overshooting at the senior partner's expense is an interpretation.
sources.note: Lower Saxony 2013: tactical votes for the FDP, a junior partner polling near the 5% threshold, were followed by a 9.9% result and a one-seat majority for the other side. A cautionary example for rescue appeals. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Wikipedia contributors (accessed 2026). 2013 German federal election (official results table). Wikipedia.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: Germany 2013: the FDP, the governing party's junior partner, won 4.76% and fell out of the Bundestag. In all, 15.7% of votes went to parties below the 5% threshold.

sources.citation: Dinas, E., Riera, P., & Roussias, N. (2015). Staying in the First League: Parliamentary Representation and the Electoral Success of Small Parties. Political Science Research and Methods 3(2): 187-204.
sources.checked: corrected: the effect sizes have now been extracted. Entering parliament raises a small party's next-election vote share by about 2 points (about 40%), but the effect is concentrated in new democracies. In established democracies, a group that includes Israel, it is not significant, so the paper does not show that a Reservists-Economic entry would create a lasting party.
sources.note: Across post-war democracies with national thresholds, small parties that just enter parliament do better at the next election, mainly in new democracies.

sources.citation: Israel National News staff (2026, 10 Oct). Gantz refuses to quit Knesset race: 'I'm running until the end'. Israel National News. Also: Berman, L. (2026, 20 Sep). Gantz to ToI: I'll drop out if I don't cross the threshold in the last week of the race. The Times of Israel.
sources.checked: corrected: the statement that Eisenkot said near-threshold lists must merge or step aside is in neither article and no source was found, so it is not used. Blue and White polled about 0.5-2% from late September to 12 October, below the line in every recent poll.
sources.note: Gantz said on 10 October he is running until the end and rejected the wasted-vote argument. On 20 September he had said he would quit if final-week polls showed Blue and White below the threshold.

sources.citation: Wikipedia contributors (accessed 2026). The Reservists (political party). Wikipedia. Also: Israel National News (2026, 12 Oct). Two polls: Hendel and Zelekha cross electoral threshold. The Jerusalem Post's report of 6 October on surplus agreements (Neev 2026) is listed separately.
sources.checked: corrected: the claimed average of about 2.7 seats from 24 September to 7 October was not reproduced. Polls split by house. Maariv, Channel 16, Kantar and Zman Yisrael had the list at 4-5 seats, while Channels 12, 13 and 14, i24 and Kan had it below the line, for an average of about 2 seats. The published 13 October forecast gives it a pass chance of about 0.21.
sources.note: Reservists-Economic is a centre-right, unaligned list founded in September 2025 that calls for a Zionist unity government without Arab or Haredi parties. Two polls on 12 October gave it 4 seats. It had no surplus agreement as of 8 October.

sources.citation: Knesset (1969, consolidated text as amended to 2026). Knesset Elections Law [Consolidated Version], 5729-1969. Hebrew Wikisource consolidation. Sections cited: 21, 24, 57, 63, 65, 67, 73, 77, 79, 81-82, 122-123, 126, 129 and 134a. Polling-room regulations as described by Aridor Hershkovitz and Shwartz Altshuler (2026), listed separately.
sources.checked: corrected: the text matches on every point checked. Fixes in use: Zehut's 2019 withdrawal took effect on day 16, after its members' vote (the deal was announced on day 19). A separate law for the 26th Knesset may set election-specific dates, so counsel should check it. A polling committee is formed without a faction only when that faction fails to name its committee chairs in time, not for any missing nominee. The 2013 case of polling-station jobs promised to activists was a committee spokesman's preliminary view and a referral to the Attorney General, not a ruling. In 2022 the Netanyahu bloc's surplus agreements together added one seat, and either of its two pairs alone would have secured it (pairing facts from Kenig 2022, listed separately).
sources.note: The election law: surplus-vote agreements (one partner per list, notice by 16 October 2026), list publication by 18 October and ballots at stations by 25 October. Polling committees have at least three factions, and a list without a seat on a committee may send one observer. No propaganda within 5 metres of a polling-station gate, no rallies, loudspeakers or broadcasts from 19:00 on the eve, and up to 5 years in prison for offering any benefit to vote or abstain.

sources.citation: Neev, K. (2026, 6 Oct, updated 8 Oct). Netanyahu's Likud, Smotrich's RZP sign surplus-vote agreement ahead of elections. The Jerusalem Post. Also: Ettinger, A. (2026). Jewish Power: Likud deal designed to keep us out of Netanyahu-Eisenkot government. Ynetnews. Ynetnews (n.d.). Ra'am and Joint List sign surplus vote agreement, pledge clean campaign.
sources.checked: corrected: the Joint List-Ra'am agreement is confirmed by Ynetnews, but its date was not. Shas-UTJ and Otzma-Amcha are assumed by the model and not yet confirmed.
sources.note: Surplus agreements signed by 8 October: Yashar-Democrats and Together-Yisrael Beytenu (September) and Likud-RZP (6 October). The Joint List and Ra'am have also signed, on a date not confirmed. Likud refused Otzma, and Reservists-Economic and Amcha had not signed. The deadline is 16 October.

sources.citation: Israel Policy Forum (2026, 24 Sep). The Electoral Threshold: What it Is and Why it Matters (IPF Explains). Israel Policy Forum.
sources.checked: verified. The turnout-to-threshold figures treat every vote as valid and the whole roll as resident, so the threshold in votes is slightly lower than stated.
sources.note: With 7.3 million registered voters, each point of turnout adds about 2,400 votes to the threshold: about 143,000 votes at 60% turnout and 191,000 at 80%. A list's survival depends on its own voters' turnout, not just its poll share.

sources.citation: Iyengar, S., Peters, M. D., & Kinder, D. R. (1982). Experimental Demonstrations of the 'Not-So-Minimal' Consequences of Television News Programs. American Political Science Review 76(4): 848-858.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: Two US lab experiments: television news decided which problems viewers rated important, and those problems then weighed more in judging the president. The foundation of agenda-setting research. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Lenz, G. S. (2009). Learning and Opinion Change, Not Priming: Reconsidering the Priming Hypothesis. American Journal of Political Science 53(4): 821-837.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: Re-analysis of four classic US cases with panel data: campaign attention to an issue mostly teaches voters their party's position, which they then adopt. Raising an issue does not automatically turn it against the incumbent.

sources.citation: Petrocik, J. R. (1996). Issue Ownership in Presidential Elections, with a 1980 Case Study. American Journal of Political Science 40(3): 825-850. Also: Ansolabehere, S., & Iyengar, S. (1994). Riding the Wave and Claiming Ownership Over Issues: The Joint Effects of Advertising and News Coverage in Campaigns. Public Opinion Quarterly 58(3): 335-357.
sources.checked: verified. No 2026 Israeli poll measures which party owns which issue, so assigning issues to change-bloc lists is an assumption.
sources.note: Parties have reputations on particular problems and gain by making the election about issues they own. US ad experiments found candidates gain most from ads on issues they own. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Bélanger, É., & Meguid, B. M. (2008). Issue salience, issue ownership, and issue-based vote choice. Electoral Studies 27(3): 477-491.
sources.checked: corrected: the paper does not say that salience without ownership helps the owner. It shows that ownership affects the vote only among voters who see the issue as important, so raising an issue's salience helps the party seen as best on it.
sources.note: Canada 1997 and 2000: seeing a party as best on an issue predicts the vote only among voters who rate that issue important. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Walgrave, S., Lefevere, J., & Nuytemans, M. (2009). Issue Ownership Stability and Change: How Political Parties Claim and Maintain Issues Through Media Appearances. Political Communication 26(2): 153-172.
sources.checked: verified. Whether the draft, the October 7 inquiry or northern recovery are unowned issues in Israel in 2026 has not been measured.
sources.note: Belgian online experiment with about 5,000 people: one news item shifted which party respondents saw as owning an issue, most on issues no party owned. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Seeberg, H. B. (2020). Issue ownership attack: how a political party can counteract a rival's issue ownership. West European Politics 43(4): 772-794.
sources.checked: corrected: moving toward the rival's position did not merely fail. On Danish agriculture it significantly raised the rival's ownership, and it had no effect on the two US issues. In the polarised US case, reframing and blame moved the attacker's own supporters more than the target's supporters.
sources.note: Danish and US survey experiments: reframing an issue or blaming the rival for poor performance cut the rival's ownership by about 7 percentage points (about a quarter of a standard deviation). Copying the rival's position did not help. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Teigen, J. M. (2013). Military Experience in Elections and Perceptions of Issue Competence. Armed Forces & Society 39(3): 415-433.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: US experiment with real ads: a military-service cue raised ratings of a candidate's security competence regardless of party, but not ratings of leadership or warmth. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Israel Democracy Institute (2013, 8 Jan). Israelis Find Netanyahu Most Suitable to Handle Security, Yachimovich for Socio-Economic Issues (Peace Index, December 2012). Press release. Also: Newman, M. (2015, 25 Jan). Cost of living tops list of election issues (Channel 10/Midgam poll). The Times of Israel.
sources.checked: verified. Leaders were rated separately on each issue, so the shares add up to more than 100%.
sources.note: In 2013 Israeli Jews rated Netanyahu best on security and Yachimovich best on the economy. In 2015 most named cost of living as the top issue, yet Netanyahu still led on security and won both elections.

sources.citation: Mohnblatt, D. (2022). Being security expert no longer key to winning Israeli elections (quoting Liron Lavi and Gideon Rahat). The Media Line, via Ynetnews.
sources.checked: verified. Expert opinion, not new data.
sources.note: Two Israeli political scientists argued before the 2022 election that security credentials no longer decide votes as they did. Voters choose a person or camp first and then credit it with security.

sources.citation: Sheafer, T., Shenhav, S. R., & Goldstein, K. (2011). Voting for Our Story: A Narrative Model of Electoral Choice in Multiparty Systems. Comparative Political Studies 44(3): 313-338.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: 2009 Knesset election: voters were more likely to choose parties whose national story matched their own, even with demographics and ideology held constant.

sources.citation: Feinstein, Y., & Ben-David, G. (2026). United or Divided? A Polarized Society's Response to War. Public Opinion Quarterly 90(3): 657-696. Also: Feinstein, Y. (2018). One flag, two rallies: Mechanisms of public opinion in Israel during the 2014 Gaza war. Social Science Research 69: 65-82. Hirsch-Hoefler, S., Canetti, D., Rapaport, C., & Hobfoll, S. E. (2016).
