principles.text: US field experiments put the persuasive effect of campaign contact in the last two months of a general election at about zero (0.13 points per person contacted, not distinguishable from zero), and ad effects fade within days. Only about 0.6-1.6% of Israeli voters say they are torn between the blocs. Across 62 elections in 10 countries, 17-29% of voters settle in the final two months, and their shifts track which issues they weigh most, not changes in their policy views. Israeli studies find the same agenda effect. In 2003 coalition considerations decided about 1 Israeli vote in 10, and foreign studies find that uncertain coalition prospects cost a party votes. The last fortnight is won by choosing the agenda and making the government on offer clear.

principles.title: Every move has a reply
principles.text: The Netanyahu bloc has the larger pool of voters who stay home. A 1-point turnout rise across its segments nets it about 11,000 votes, against about 6,700 for the change bloc from the same rise across its own. It has shown it can add votes fast: Likud gained about 239,000 votes between September 2019 and March 2020, though about a third of that matched the fall of Yamina and Otzma. Visible campaigns against a group's turnout have woken that group: Arab turnout rose from 49% to 59% after Likud's 2019 camera campaign, though the Joint List's reunion also played a part. In the model, 25,000 extra Netanyahu-bloc votes cost about 1.3 points of the change-led chance, close to the 1.7 that 25,000 extra change votes gain. Judge every visible tactic by the reaction it provokes as well as the votes it wins.

principles.title: The election does not end on 27 October
principles.text: Neither the Netanyahu bloc nor the change lists with Ra'am reach 61 in about six simulations in ten, and a repeat election is the most likely single outcome, at about 47%. The President tasks whoever has the best chance of forming a government, guided by recommendations and list size, neither of which binds him. In 2009 President Peres passed over the leader of the largest list. If formation fails, the legal timetable points to a new election in April or May 2027. One agreed recommendation, a clear government on offer and supporter lists that can be used again are part of winning, not an afterthought.

levers.title: Blue and White withdraws and endorses
levers.summary: Blue and White (Gantz) sits at about 0.6% in the forecast and clears the threshold in about 1% of simulations, so almost all of its roughly 31,000 votes are on course to be wasted. If it withdrew and endorsed, and its voters split as in 2022 (60% Yashar, 25% Together, 15% stay home), the model adds about 1.7 points to the change-led chance, 0.91 points to the chance of denying Netanyahu 61 and 0.43 change seats. With half a point of the vote also leaving Likud, the gain is about 4.8 points.
levers.evidence: Gantz said on 10 October that he is running until the end. He called the wasted-vote argument a lie, said he belongs to neither bloc and claimed, without data, at least six seats' worth of potential voters. Senior opposition figures had pressed him to quit. On 20 September he had said he would stop if final-week polls showed him below the threshold, and every recent poll has the party at about 0.5-2%. Leaders' deals rarely deliver their voters. After Zehut withdrew in 2019 for a cabinet promise, only about 29% of its voters went to Likud, and only about 21% of Kulanu's voters followed Kahlon into Likud. Mergers fare little better: five of seven Jewish-sector unions since 2013 kept only 64-85% of their parts' combined vote. The model's split sends none of Blue and White's voters to Likud, the favourable end. The coordination desk's runs with about a quarter going to Likud and a fifth staying home roughly halve the gain in change seats, to about 0.2. Timing binds. Lists are published on Sun 18 Oct, ballots are printed only for published lists, and the desk found no clear legal rule for a later withdrawal. Zehut's exit 16 days out took it off the ballot. A list below 1% of the vote gets no state election funding and must repay any advance it drew. In foreign experiments, voters who believe their party has no chance defect far more often, by up to 40 points in one German study.
levers.feasibility_note: Low. Gantz has said publicly that he will run to the end, and pressure from senior opposition figures has not moved him. The only clean window is before the lists are published on Sun 18 Oct, five days away, and his own trigger, the final-week polls, comes after the ballots are printed. One private approach by a senior envoy is worth making. A public pressure campaign is not. If he declines, the value moves to rescue: media and calls to identified Blue and White voters around the final published polls on Fri 23 Oct.
levers.timing: Approach by Fri 16 Oct. Lists published Sun 18 Oct. Rescue media and calls Fri 23 to Mon 26 Oct.
levers.owner: Eisenkot with Bennett and Lapid decide. One senior envoy approaches Gantz. The joint message group runs rescue.
actions: Make one private approach through a single senior envoy by Fri 16 Oct. Offer public credit and a visible role in the campaign, not an ultimatum. Election counsel reviews any written undertaking.
Ask election counsel now whether a withdrawal after Sun 18 Oct would take the list off the ballot, including under the special-provisions law for this election.
If Gantz endorses, hold one joint appearance and run a short endorsement ad aimed at his voters. Any joint spending needs both lists' counsel and treasurers.
Do not ask for or accept Blue and White's voter lists unless election counsel clears it in writing.

If he stays in, run rescue through media and calls to identified Blue and White voters, built on threshold arithmetic. Friday 23 Oct creative that quotes a poll carries the survey details the law requires and comes down before Sat 24 Oct. From Sat 24 Oct, no poll figures in any material.
risks: Public pressure can harden Gantz and offend his voters, who are the people the bloc wants.
An exit after Sun 18 Oct may leave Blue and White's slips in the booth, and votes cast for it would be wasted.
Voters follow their own views, not the leader's deal. Some will go to Likud or stay home.

levers.title: Reservists-Economic withdraws
levers.summary: Reservists-Economic (Hendel and Zelekha) is a right-of-centre, reservist-branded list at about 1.7% in the forecast, clearing the threshold in about 21% of simulations. If it withdrew and 60% of its roughly 80,000 voters went to change lists, the change-led chance would rise about 1.6 points, but the chance of denying Netanyahu 61 would fall about 0.84 points. If most went right (35% to change lists), the change-led chance would fall about 1.0 point and the blocking chance about 3.0 points, so this is not a lever to pull.
levers.evidence: The list's success cuts both ways. In the draws where it passes, the Netanyahu bloc reaches 61 in about 7.3% against 14.7% where it fails, but the change lists hold about 2.2 fewer seats. Its stated terms fit only a Zionist-only change coalition or a unity government: Hendel wants a Zionist government only, says he will not complete a majority with haredi parties or be the 61st seat of a government that depends on Arab parties, and says Netanyahu should go. The list has not ruled out working with Netanyahu. Published polls split by house: some give it 4-5 seats, others put it below the line, about 2 seats on average. Final polls are a poor guide near the line. Since 2009, lists averaging 3.5-4.5 seats in the final three weeks failed 22% of the time, and lists averaging 0.5-3.5 seats survived more than half the time. No published data show where its voters came from or would go. Past exits scattered voters by their own views, so for a right-of-centre list the pessimistic split is plausible. Hendel withdrew his previous list in 2022, but before lists closed. A list that wins more than 1% receives one unit of state election funding, about NIS 1.8 million, a reason to stay in. In a 2024 poll of reservists who fought in the war, 77% said Haredi exemptions are no longer affordable, so this constituency overlaps with the bloc's equal-burden message.
levers.feasibility_note: Low, and not worth trying. The list polls near the line, has a funding reason to stay in, and the choice belongs to its leaders and voters. The model cannot say whether an exit would help or hurt, because that depends on where its voters go, and there are no data on that. What the bloc controls is tone. Its equal-burden message and the Reservists share a constituency, and contempt for either would cost both.
levers.timing: Tone from now to Mon 26 Oct. No approach planned. Post-election contact through the coalition track.
levers.owner: The four list leaders set the tone. The joint message group enforces it.
actions: Do not campaign for the list's exit and do not attack it. Describe it as a right-of-centre, reservist-branded list, and speak of its voters with respect.

Under the change-led objective only, and only if the Fri 23 Oct polls show the list well below the line, calls to identified Reservists voters may use threshold arithmetic. Under the blocking objective, skip them: in the model they lower the chance of denying Netanyahu 61.
Treat the list as a possible partner after the vote. Its stated conditions fit a Zionist-only change coalition or a unity government (see the Coalition page).
Reach reservists as civilians only: never through IDF units, bases, unit chat groups or employers, and never with uniforms or military imagery.
risks: Pressure on the list could push its voters right, the split that costs both objectives.
Dismissive language about reservists or about the list would undercut the bloc's own equal-burden message.

levers.title: Move soft Likud voters on the draft and October 7 accountability
levers.summary: A vote that leaves Likud for a change list is worth nearly two new change votes. Half a point of the national vote, about 24,000 voters or one Likud voter in 40, adds about 3.1 points to the change-led chance (deny-61 +1.9, +0.67 change seats). One point adds about 6.3 and two points about 13, because each extra half point lands closer to 61.
levers.evidence: The pool exists. In May only 58% of 2022 Likud voters said they would definitely vote Likud again, and October 7 (37%) and the draft (23%) were their main reasons to consider switching. About 71% of Jews oppose the law freezing arrests of yeshiva students who do not report for service. Two-thirds of voters say the October 7 failures have not been fixed, and more trust an Eisenkot-led government to fix them than Netanyahu's (48% against 30%). Coalition voters are split: 27% say Netanyahu bears a great deal of responsibility, and 37-52% back a state commission, depending on the survey. Late persuasion is hard. Only about 0.6-1.6% of voters say they are torn between the blocs. US field experiments find that contact in the last two months persuades almost no one, and ad effects fade within days. The French exception: door canvassing in Hollande's 2012 campaign raised his vote share by just under a point where canvassers were sent, without changing turnout. Across 62 elections in 10 countries, late deciders moved with the issues they weighed, and in Canadian data an issue helped the side seen as best on it only when voters thought it mattered. In foreign experiments, blaming a rival for poor performance or reframing the issue cut the rival's ownership by about 7 points out of 100, while copying the rival's position did not help and in one case backfired. In the polarised US case the effect was larger among the attacker's own supporters, so the dent among Likud voters may be smaller.
levers.feasibility_note: Low for a full point, possible for less. Even a tenth of the half-point scenario, about 2,400 switchers, would be worth more than twice the whole realistic field programme on the model's rates. The lever is the national campaign's agenda, which is being spent anyway: what the four lists talk about for the last 14 days, and who says it. That needs the four leaders to agree one closing argument this week. A full point or more would probably need an event the campaign does not control.
levers.timing: Agree the closing argument by Thu 15 Oct. Broadcast and rally propaganda runs to 19:00 Mon 26 Oct.
levers.owner: The four list leaders agree. The joint message group and each list's media team execute.
actions: Close on two issues the bloc can own with soft Likud voters: an equal share of service and accountability for October 7. Keep cost of living for undecided voters, who name it as their first concern.
Blame performance and reframe. Do not copy Likud's positions. Frame the draft as equal burden, never as contempt for Haredi citizens.

Choose messengers soft Likud voters trust: former Likud voters, traditional and religious public figures, and reservists speaking as civilians. In a US study, campaign volunteers were unrepresentative of the voters they tried to persuade.
Pretest ads quickly and put the money behind the best ones. In US campaigns' own tests, ads varied by about half around the average effect.
In the field programme, persuasion happens only inside door conversations on positive stations and in calls to identified soft voters (see the Field pages).
risks: Messages that sound like contempt for Likud voters push them back. In US experiments, cues from out-party leaders polarised.
Persuasive door contact may backfire: in one US experiment it possibly lowered support and almost certainly did not raise it.
In 2015 Likud's late gains came mostly from inside its own bloc after final-days appeals. Expect a 'gevalt' close.

levers.title: Win traditional voters who have voted Shas
levers.summary: Half a point of the vote moving from Shas and UTJ to change lists is worth about as much as half a point from Likud: about 2.8 points on the change-led chance (deny-61 +2.0, +0.68 change seats). The realistic pool is traditional (masorti) voters who have voted Shas, not Haredi communities, whose vote is cohesive.
levers.evidence: Haredi voters stay with their lists: 86% voted for Haredi lists in 2022. Shas, by contrast, has been losing moderately traditional, working-class voters over the draft crisis, to Otzma, Likud and Yashar, and Eisenkot says he meets would-be Shas defectors in Kiryat Shmona, Shlomi and Or Yehuda. About 15% of Otzma's current voters say they voted Shas in 2022. Shas is fighting back by reconciling Deri with Rabbi Yitzhak Yosef and using religious imagery. Yashar already runs local structures in Likud strongholds such as Dimona. A US experiment found that religious coded language reached religious voters without costing support among others. There is no Israeli evidence on persuading Shas voters late in a campaign.
levers.feasibility_note: Low. Many traditional voters leaving Shas are going to Otzma or Likud, which does nothing for the bloc, and Shas is fighting to hold them. The bloc can reach this pool only through messengers from it, in the towns where Eisenkot is already meeting them, and without any message that sounds like an attack on Haredi people.
levers.owner: Yashar's outreach to traditional voters, with local traditional figures. The joint message group checks tone.
actions: Speak to traditional voters about cost of living, the north and an equal share of service, in their own idiom and with respect for Shas and its rabbis.
Use local traditional figures as messengers in the periphery towns where the bloc already has a presence.
Keep this a persuasion effort. Do not send door teams into Netanyahu-bloc strongholds: the model shows door canvassing there nets votes for the other side.
risks: A draft message heard as contempt for Haredim helps Shas and UTJ mobilise their own voters.
Most voters who leave Shas may still choose Otzma or Likud.

levers.title: Raise change-supporter turnout beyond the field programme
levers.summary: Extra turnout among change supporters, through relational organising and supporters' own networks rather than door teams. 25,000 extra change-list votes, about 1.3% more than the lists' projected vote, add about 1.7 points to the change-led chance (deny-61 +1.0, +0.44 seats), and 50,000 add about 3.4 (deny-61 +2.0, +0.86 seats). That is about 15 to 30 times what a 400,000-contact field programme buys.
levers.evidence: Friend-to-friend contact is the one tactic with large measured effects at high baseline turnout: about 8 points per message actually received in a 2018 US trial where the baseline was about 76%. A supervised US 'captain' pilot, in a low-salience election, raised turnout 13 points. Impersonal tools do little when salience is high. Social-pressure mail had no effect on voters above 60% prior propensity, and an $8.9 million US social-media programme had no average effect on turnout. Messages that stress high expected turnout work better than complaints about low turnout. The enthusiasm gap favours the bloc: in October, 86% of opposition supporters were certain to vote, against 81% of coalition supporters. The danger is breadth. A uniform national turnout rise nets the Netanyahu bloc about 3,300 votes per point, so turnout work must reach identified change supporters, not everyone. Students and young voters can vote only at the station where they are registered, and intercity buses and trains are free from 20:00 on Mon 26 Oct. Messages a list segments by any personal characteristic, on any channel, count as direct mail and must carry the notices the privacy rules require.
levers.feasibility_note: Low for 25,000, and lower still for 50,000. The one large effect measured at a high baseline is about 8 points per message actually received, in a single US trial. For Israel's high-salience race the research desk's planning figure is about 3 points per friend asked (range 1-8). On that figure 25,000 extra votes need on the order of 800,000 friend asks, about 80,000 volunteers and active supporters each reminding ten people they know, from their own phones, in the final week. At the US trial's rate it would be about 300,000. This is our arithmetic on foreign studies, so treat it as an order of magnitude, and plan for a smaller gain. The four lists can launch it in days if they start this week, and it works through people's own networks rather than broadcasts that also reach Netanyahu-bloc voters.
levers.timing: Recruit from Thu 15 Oct. Personal reminders in the final week, Tue 20 to Tue 27 Oct.
levers.owner: The four campaign managers, each through its own volunteers, under one shared rulebook.
actions: Ask every volunteer and active supporter to name about ten people and remind them personally in the final week, from their own phones and contacts.
Say that people are voting. Do not complain that turnout is low.
Messages sent from a list's database carry the direct-mail notices. No voter-level data passes between lists without written clearance from election counsel.
Remind students and young voters where they are registered and that intercity buses and trains are free from 20:00 Mon 26 Oct. The bloc organises no rides.
Reach soldiers and reservists as civilians, through family and friends, never through IDF units, bases or employers.
risks: Broad appeals and public turnout counts wake Netanyahu-bloc voters, who are the larger pool.
Expat flights are a legal and narrative target: Likud's petition ended in a compromise with no ticket subsidies and no new flights. Keep the lists away from any transport or benefit.
Bulk or automated sending gets WhatsApp accounts blocked.

levers.title: Keep Ra'am above the line by doing no harm
levers.summary: Ra'am clears the threshold in about 80% of simulations, and whether it passes is one of the largest threshold swings in the forecast, alongside RZP-Zehut and Amcha. Half a point of the vote moving from the Joint List to Ra'am adds about 1.1 points to the change-led chance (deny-61 +0.40, -0.09 change seats). That movement is the Arab lists' own business, and the bloc's lever is to do nothing that pushes Ra'am down.
levers.evidence: Ra'am has finished just above the line in each of its last three runs: 3.33%, 3.79% and 4.07%. The Netanyahu bloc reaches 61 in about 9.7% of the draws where Ra'am passes and 27% where it fails, a correlation that partly reflects Arab turnout. The election committee's ban on Ra'am was overturned unanimously by the Supreme Court on 2 October, and ynet reports that Ra'am and the Joint List have signed a surplus agreement. Polls are a poor guide near the line: Ra'am averaged 1.7 seats in the final 2021 polls and won 4. Campaigns that paint reliance on Arab parties as illegitimate may depress Arab turnout, and Likud's 2019 camera campaign was followed by a rise in Arab turnout. The constraint runs the other way too: 61% of Jews oppose including Ra'am in the next government.
levers.feasibility_note: High, because it asks for restraint, not action. The four lists control only their own words. They should neither attack Ra'am nor campaign on bringing it in, which most Jewish voters oppose. Whether to support Arab-sector turnout at all is a separate leadership decision (see below).
levers.owner: The four list leaders. The joint message group enforces.
actions: No attacks on Ra'am, or on Arab citizens' right to vote and take part. Answer Likud's 'dependence on Arab parties' line with the bloc's own coalition terms (see the Coalition page), not by denigrating Arab parties.
A change list's own outreach to Arab voters is its own decision. It should not aim at Ra'am's voters while Ra'am sits near the line.
risks: Embracing Ra'am publicly costs Jewish votes and feeds Likud's strongest wedge.
Ra'am's result depends mostly on Arab turnout and the Arab lists' own campaigns, which the bloc does not control.

levers.title: Stop competing for each other's voters
levers.summary: While all four change lists are safe, votes moving between them are worth almost nothing: half a point moving from Yashar to the Democrats changes the change-led chance by 0.01 points (deny-61 -0.01). Every change list clears the line in about 97% of simulations or more. The value lies in not letting a fight for the largest list push Yisrael Beytenu or the Democrats toward the line, as happened to Meretz in 2022.
levers.evidence: In 2022 Yesh Atid took about 18% of Meretz's 2021 voters, roughly 36,000 votes, about nine times the roughly 4,000 votes Meretz lacked. A change list failing is rare but costly: in the rare draws where Yisrael Beytenu or the Democrats miss, the Netanyahu bloc reaches 61 in about 37% and 54% of them. The fight is live: Together is trying to win back former Yesh Atid voters who moved to Yashar. Being the largest list does not decide who forms the government, since the President tasks whoever has the best chance and in 2009 passed over the largest list. The two change surplus agreements already add about 0.56 expected change seats. Insurance appeals can overshoot: in Lower Saxony in 2013 the junior partner polled near 5%, won 9.9%, and its senior partner lost power, though the source does not establish the counterfactual. In foreign studies, uncertain coalition prospects cost a party votes.
levers.feasibility_note: High. It needs the four campaign chiefs to agree a no-poaching rule this week and to hold it after each weekend's polls. Turf is already split by each station's lead change list on the Field pages.
levers.timing: Agree by Thu 15 Oct. Review after the polls of Fri 16 and Fri 23 Oct.
actions: No 'biggest party' appeals aimed at allies' voters, and no attack ads inside the bloc.
Split field turf by each station's lead change list (Field pages).
Hold insurance appeals in reserve. Use them only if a change list falls toward the line in the final published polls, and aim them at the bloc's own voters.
Joint spending needs both lists' counsel and treasurers. Shared voter data needs written clearance from election counsel.
risks: Over-insurance can starve the list that gives the votes.
A visible fight inside the bloc tells soft voters the government on offer is unstable.

levers.title: Show one clear government on offer
levers.summary: The model has no scenario for this lever, and the Coalition page sets out the paths in detail. On the forecast, the change lists reach 61 alone in about 6.9% of simulations and with Ra'am in about 26%. The formation model gives a change-led government about 22%, a unity government with Likud but without Netanyahu about 11%, and a repeat election about 47%.
levers.evidence: Coalition expectations shape Israeli votes. In 2003 coalition considerations decided about 1 vote in 10. In 2006 voters who expected their party to stay out of government deserted it for the least-bad viable partner, and in 2019-20 voters switched to influence who would form the government. In foreign studies, uncertain coalition prospects lower a party's vote, by about 11 points of vote probability between the most and least certain cases, and explicit coalition signals raise the weight voters give to coalition considerations. In a German experiment, strictly strategic voting was a minority behaviour. The constraints are real: 61% of Jews oppose including Ra'am, while 53% of voters support including a haredi party. Shas and UTJ reportedly lean toward recommending nobody and sitting out a year. On the forecast medians, a single change candidate would have about 52 recommendations, against 36 for Netanyahu from Likud, Otzma and RZP, or 53 if Shas and UTJ recommend him. Inoculating voters against an expected attack builds resistance that lasts about two weeks.
levers.feasibility_note: Medium. It needs four leaders, two of whom want the premiership, to agree one name for the President and one set of conditions for each partner this week. They do not need to agree everything. An agreed recommendation and agreed conditions would remove most of the uncertainty that costs votes.
levers.timing: Agree by Thu 15 Oct. Announce by Sun 18 Oct. Recommendations to the President after the results.
levers.owner: Eisenkot, Bennett and Lapid, Golan and Liberman.
actions: Agree one name to recommend to the President.
State conditions, not bans, for each path to 61: the Reservists, Ra'am inside the coalition or outside it, a haredi party, or a Likud after Netanyahu (see the Coalition page).
Answer the 'dependence on Arab parties' attack with the bloc's own terms before Likud's final push, not with silence.
Joint coalition advertising is cross-list spending: both lists' counsel and treasurers sign off.
risks: Bans announced now may close the only path to 61 later.
Signals toward Ra'am cost Jewish votes, and signals toward haredi parties blunt the equal-burden message.

levers.title: Run the field programme where it nets votes
levers.summary: Door conversations in polling-station areas where extra turnout and persuasion net change-bloc votes, plus calls and friend-to-friend asks to identified voters (see the Field pages: Playbook and Planner). A realistic 150,000-400,000 completed contacts is worth about 760-1,700 net votes for a change-led government, roughly 0.05-0.12 points, and about 930-1,800 under the blocking objective. Across the model's assumption sets the same plans range from about 420 to 4,300 net votes.
levers.evidence: Personal contact is the best-supported turnout tactic, but its effect shrinks in high-salience elections and outside the US. US canvassing in high-salience races raised turnout about 3 points per completed conversation. Pooled European canvassing is about 0.8 points and not distinguishable from zero. Effects are largest where baseline turnout is 30-50% and near zero above 70%. About 60% of the effect reaches the other voter in a two-voter household. In one US study, only calls made in the final week worked. Small as it is, the field margin can decide a threshold: Meretz missed by 4,061 votes in 2022. Election-day rules bind everyone: no propaganda within 5 metres of a polling place, and party representatives may not tell their parties which voters have voted. Gifts, entertainment and food tied to propaganda are banned.
levers.feasibility_note: High. The bloc controls it, the planner allocates it, and 14 days is enough to run it. Its value is at the margin: a threshold, a remainder seat, the 61st seat. It should not absorb leaders' time that belongs to the national levers above.
levers.timing: Now to Tue 27 Oct, with most contacts in the final ten days.
levers.owner: Each list's field director on its own lead-list turf, with one joint field desk running the planner.
actions: Send door teams only to polling-station areas where the model shows positive value. Never canvass Netanyahu-bloc strongholds, where door work nets votes for the other side.
In supporter-list ground, Netanyahu-majority cities with many change voters, reach identified supporters by calls, texts and friend-to-friend asks, not doors.
Split turf by each station's lead change list. No voter-level data passes between lists without written clearance from election counsel.
Persuade only inside door conversations on positive stations and by calls to identified soft Netanyahu-bloc voters. Run rescue by calls and media only.
Plan nothing in Arab localities or in stations where Arab lists lead. Hold Druze towns out until the candidate check and a Druze poll are done.
No organised rides, no gifts, no food or entertainment tied to campaigning, and nothing within 5 metres of a polling place on election day.
risks: Canvassing the wrong turf mobilises the other side.
Turf disputes between the four lists waste the last week.

levers.title: Protect the count
levers.summary: The model has no scenario for this lever. In Israel vote protection means accurate counting, valid ballots and documented objections, not watching voters. With RZP-Zehut, Otzma and Ra'am near the line and several seats decided by remainders, a few hundred votes can move a seat.
levers.evidence: In April 2019 the final count, with corrections and the double-envelope votes, moved a seat from Likud to UTJ, which had been several hundred ballots short. In September 2019 the committee annulled six stations for apparent tampering, and with other corrections a seat moved from UTJ to Likud. About 0.5-0.7% of ballots are invalid, roughly 30,000 in 2022, and double-envelope ballots are invalid more often (0.88% against 0.59%). Double envelopes were almost a tenth of all ballots in 2022 and are counted centrally after election night. Factions can still name and replace their committee members, and a list with no seat on a committee may send one observer. In foreign studies, observers reduce fraud at the stations they cover but can displace it to others, and announcing that result sheets will be photographed cut tampering in Afghanistan, though the legality of photographing protocols here is an open question. The 2019 hidden cameras in Arab polling stations show what not to do: a Likud contractor claimed credit for low Arab turnout, no effect was established, and Arab turnout rose at the next election.
levers.feasibility_note: High. Committee composition was fixed on 17 September, but the factions can still fill and replace their seats. Staffing, training and a count desk can be ready in ten days if the four lists share one staffing map.
levers.timing: Staffing map by Thu 22 Oct. Training Sat 24 to Mon 26 Oct. Count desk from 22:00 Tue 27 Oct to the final results.
levers.owner: Each list's election-day director and election counsel, through one joint count desk.
actions: Fill every committee seat and alternate held by the bloc's outgoing-Knesset factions, and send a change-list observer wherever no allied faction has a seat. A new list such as Yashar may have observers only.
Train members on valid-ballot rules and on checking and signing the protocol.
Reconcile each signed protocol with the published station result, and file objections in writing.
Ask election counsel before anyone photographs a protocol.
Follow the double-envelope count after election night.
Do not film voters, report who has voted, or post anyone to watch a community.
risks: Observers who act as watchers of voters invite backlash and legal action.
A thin staffing map leaves the stations that matter uncovered.

levers.title: Arab-sector turnout: a leadership decision
levers.summary: Whether the change bloc supports Arab-sector turnout at all is a leadership decision, not a field one. In the model, Arab turnout 5 points higher (about 46,000 more votes for the Joint List and Ra'am) lowers the change-led chance by about 1.4 points but raises the chance of denying Netanyahu 61 by about 2.1 points, and costs the change lists about 0.58 seats. The two objectives point in opposite directions.
levers.evidence: Arab turnout was 53.2% in 2022. From 2013 to 2021 it rose only when the Arab parties ran together, though in 2022 it rose despite a three-way split. A May 2026 survey put expected turnout at about 53% with separate lists, and a pollster associates this year's configuration, a three-party Joint List with Ra'am separate, with about 59%. Survey turnout figures for Arab citizens are unreliable, and the one forecast error the research could verify went the other way (56% forecast, 59% actual in September 2019), so treat these as rough guides, not bounds. About 80% of Arab respondents rank crime and violence first. Campaigns that paint reliance on Arab parties as illegitimate may depress Arab turnout, while visible attempts to suppress it were followed by backlash in 2019. Rules bind anyone who acts: a group that spends more than about NIS 120,000 on election activity must first register with the State Comptroller and publish its donations, and Likud has already taken visible turnout operations to the election committee.
levers.feasibility_note: Low as a lever. Arab turnout depends mostly on the Arab lists' own campaigns, crime and unity, which the bloc does not control. The bloc runs and brands no turnout work in Arab localities or in polling stations where Arab lists lead, and the atlas publishes no town-level Arab targets. Any support leadership chooses to give is independent, transparent and cleared by election counsel. The model's reverse scenario is context only: the bloc never works to lower anyone's turnout. What it controls in every case is its own language.
levers.owner: The four list leaders, with election counsel.
actions: Decide at leadership level, with election counsel, which objective governs this question, and record the decision.

If any support is given, it goes only to independent, transparent, partner-led civic work that is registered as the law requires. Never change-bloc-run or branded activity, never organised rides, never gifts.
Whatever the decision, speak of Arab citizens and their vote with respect, and never treat their participation as a threat.
risks: Any change-bloc-branded activity in Arab towns would feed Likud's 'dependence on Arab parties' attack and its election-day turnout alarms.
Higher Arab turnout dilutes change-list seats and, in the model, lowers the change-led chance.

levers.title: Do not wake the other side
levers.summary: Every Netanyahu-bloc voter the campaign wakes cancels much of what a mobilised change voter adds. In the model, 25,000 extra Netanyahu-bloc votes cost about 1.3 points of the change-led chance (deny-61 -1.3, -0.27 change seats), against the 1.7 points that 25,000 extra change votes gain. On the blocking objective the loss is larger than the gain (1.3 against 1.0).
levers.evidence: The Netanyahu bloc holds the larger pool of low-turnout voters. A 1-point turnout rise across its segments nets it about 11,000 votes, against about 6,700 for the change bloc from the same rise across its own. On the current budgets, a rise of about 0.07-0.16 points across its segments would cancel the realistic field programme. Likud gained about 239,000 votes between September 2019 and March 2020, though about a third of that matched the fall of Yamina and Otzma. It is again targeting low-turnout stations where it wins about half the vote, and it plans to use the committee's election-day station turnout releases, due at least four times during the day, to rally its base by pointing to high turnout in change-bloc areas and Arab communities. Visible opposition mobilisation has repeatedly become a Likud narrative and a legal target, from V15 in 2015 to the 2026 expat flights. In US experiments, threats to a party's standing rouse its strongest identifiers, though negative campaigning in general does not depress turnout. The model's haredi-turnout scenario is context, not a lever. It shows how much rides on a turnout the bloc does not control and must not try to lower: a 10% fall in Shas and UTJ votes would move the change-led chance by about 3.2 points. Paying voters to abstain is a crime, and the committee has already barred one group from offering money to stay home.
levers.feasibility_note: High. This is about the bloc's own conduct, which it fully controls: turnout work aimed at identified supporters, no door teams in Netanyahu-bloc strongholds, no triumphalism and no rhetoric against any community.
levers.timing: Now to 22:00 Tue 27 Oct, with an election-day reply plan for each turnout release.
levers.owner: The joint message group, with each list's field and digital leads.
actions: Keep turnout work aimed at identified supporters through calls and their own networks.
Do not publish or amplify turnout figures from change-leaning areas on election day. Expect Likud to use the committee's releases, and have a reply ready that attacks no community.
No 'we are winning' messages in the final week. They threaten Likud's strongest identifiers and can relax the bloc's own voters.
Never cast Haredim, Arab citizens or Likud voters as the enemy in any message.
risks: One viral clip of contempt can undo a week of field work.
Likud's election-day alarm is a known play. In 2015 an 'Arab voters in droves' message went out on election day, though no causal estimate of its effect exists.

levers.title: The right consolidates
levers.summary: If Amcha (Ofer Winter) withdrew, with about 100,000 votes moving 80% to Likud and Otzma and 20% to change lists, the change-led chance would fall about 1.0 point. The deny-61 effect has the opposite sign in the model (+0.95 points): the exit removes some narrow Netanyahu majorities, in part because a fifth of Amcha's voters go to change lists. This is model arithmetic, not a forecast.
levers.evidence: Amcha clears the line in about 28% of simulations. Winter says he will recommend Netanyahu and join a Netanyahu government only if a national-service law passes first. Its voters come almost entirely from Likud and RZP-Otzma. The Netanyahu bloc's path to 61 runs through its own small lists: it reaches 61 in about 26% of the draws where Amcha passes against 8.2% where it fails, and the pattern is the same for RZP and Otzma, though these are correlations. Late consolidation is a Likud pattern: in 2015 it won 30 seats after final polls of 20-23, with its gains coming mostly from inside its own bloc. In foreign experiments, insurance votes flow to a small partner when polls show it just below the line.
levers.feasibility_note: Low. The bloc cannot prevent consolidation on the right and should not try. It can avoid helping it: talking up the right's threshold troubles hands Likud its 'gevalt' argument.
levers.timing: Watch through Fri 23 Oct. Have a reply ready for a late 'gevalt' close.
actions: Do not talk in public about the threshold chances of RZP, Otzma or Amcha.
Prepare a reply to a late Likud 'gevalt' appeal that speaks to soft Likud voters about the draft and October 7, not about the right's arithmetic.
risks: Consolidation lowers the change-led chance even as it lowers the chance of a Netanyahu 61.
A late consolidation can make the final polls misleading, as in 2015.

levers.title: Stay inside the law and off the petition list
levers.summary: The model has no scenario for this lever. Petitions, removal orders and data or finance breaches cost assets and news cycles in the last week, and fines and debts later. Likud has already won orders against Yashar and Together material.
levers.evidence: The election committee's chair ordered Yashar to remove a video with AI-generated soldiers and ordered Bennett to cut IDF segments from a campaign video, and Likud has petitioned against three Yashar videos about Netanyahu's conduct before October 7. AI-made or altered content must carry a clear disclosure under rules issued on 26 July, and every election ad must name who commissioned it. Published polls must state who commissioned and conducted them, the dates, the sample and the margin of error, and no new poll may be published from the end of Friday 23 October until polls close. Spending by bodies linked to a party counts as party spending. The voter register may be used only for this election, never passed on, and must be deleted afterwards. The Privacy Protection Authority can now fine per person in a database, and targeted messages count as direct mail that must carry notices. In 2022 the State Comptroller found six factions had enriched register data from commercial firms without checking its source. Comptroller fines have arrived one and a half to more than two years after the vote. A single wrongful WhatsApp block can disrupt a whole operation.
levers.feasibility_note: High. Every item is within the bloc's control. It needs one counsel sign-off rule for all four lists, applied to every ad, message flow and joint activity for the next 14 days.
levers.timing: Rules in force now. Poll ban from Sat 24 Oct. Register deletion after the results.
levers.owner: Each list's election counsel and treasurer, through one joint compliance channel.
actions: Counsel signs off every ad before it runs: disclosure labels on AI content, the sponsor line, no IDF uniforms or units, and no images of fallen or wounded soldiers without written consent.
Friday 23 Oct creative that quotes a poll carries the legally required survey details and comes down before Sat 24 Oct. No poll figures in campaign material from Sat 24 Oct.
Cross-list or joint spending only with both lists' counsel and treasurers.
No voter-level data between lists without written clearance from election counsel, and no enriched data whose source cannot be shown.
Avoid bulk or automated WhatsApp sending, and agree a fast escalation route for wrongful blocks.
risks: A removal order in the final week costs a news cycle at the worst moment.
Fines and deficits land on the lists long after the campaign has ended.

messaging.intro: Messaging is the largest lever the bloc can still pull in the last two weeks, but its yield is uncertain: few voters are torn between the blocs, and in US field tests late campaign contact has rarely persuaded anyone. The stakes are large. In the scenario engine, half a point of the national vote (about 24,000 votes) moving from Likud to the four change lists lifts the chance of a change-led government, now about 22%, by 3.1 points. A realistic field programme adds about 0.05 to 0.12 points. The job is therefore to change which issues soft Netanyahu-bloc and traditional voters weigh, through messengers they trust, without waking the other side's base. Each section separates what the research shows from our judgement, and says where the evidence is foreign or missing.

principles.title: Win the agenda, not the argument
principles.text: Evidence: in US experiments, TV news decided which problems viewers rated important and how much weight those problems carried when they judged the president. Across four Israeli elections, TV coverage drove which issue people named as the top problem and primed their vote intentions. In 62 elections in 10 countries, 17-29% of voters decided in the final two months, and their shifts followed issue priorities and beliefs about candidates, not policy views. Campaign contact within two months of a US general election persuaded almost no one (pooled effect 0.13 points). In N12's 9 Oct poll only about 0.6% of voters were torn between the blocs, and 5% of Netanyahu-bloc intenders said they would switch against 2% the other way. Raising an issue helps the side voters already see as best on it, and only among voters who rate it important (Canada). Model: half a point of the vote moving from Likud to the change lists adds 3.1 points to the chance of a change-led government, and a full point adds 6.3. Judgement: close on the draft and October 7 accountability, keep cost of living as the lead for undecided voters and right-wing voters who name it first, and pair each with a messenger voters trust to deliver on it.

principles.title: Contest competence and accountability, not identity
principles.text: Evidence: Israeli votes have long been organised by collective identity: territory and security, the Jewish character of the state and religion. In 2009 voters chose parties whose national story matched their own. Support for the 2023 judicial overhaul tracked attachment to Netanyahu and hostility to partisan opponents (Israeli panel, 2023). Before the 2022 election two Israeli political scientists argued that voters credit security to the side they have already chosen, which is why former chiefs of staff gained little. In an Italian field experiment, messages about a mayor's competence and record moved more votes than ideological ones. Voters are easier to move on candidates they know less about (US), and Netanyahu is fully known. In 2006, 31% of 2003 Likud voters voted Kadima, and more than half of those switchers cited Sharon personally. Judgement: argue about who prepared, who failed and who can run the state. Introduce Eisenkot, Bennett and Liberman through their records. Do not fight on identity, where Likud is strongest.

principles.title: Match the messenger to the audience
principles.text: Evidence: a frame moves opinion only when listeners find its source credible, and a named out-party leader pushes partisans away from a policy (US experiments). Criticism from inside a voter's own camp persuades more than criticism from the other side (US). A liberal group's endorsement worked as a negative cue for Republicans in a US field test. Senior military voices move opinion most when they oppose a specific decision, yet about 186 retired Israeli generals and security chiefs campaigned against Netanyahu in 2015 and he won. Campaign volunteers are often unrepresentative of the voters they contact, and standard management did not fix it (US). No Israeli experiment on messengers was found. Judgement: soft-right, traditional and national-religious voters should hear Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman, Matan Kahana, local traditional figures, and former security chiefs speaking as civilians about specific decisions. Golan and Lapid speak to the base. Choose local, traditional or reservist volunteers for persuasion calls.

principles.title: Do not wake the other side
principles.text: Evidence: in US experiments, threats to a party's standing made its strong identifiers angrier, and anger mobilises. Strong dislike of a party raises turnout by about 9 points across 17 European PR systems. Israel's own results suggest how big the response can be. After Likud's 2019 hidden-camera campaign in Arab polling stations, Arab-list votes rose 39.5% while all votes rose 2.9%, though the Joint List's reunification also played a part. Likud added about 240,000 votes between September 2019 and March 2020, about a third of it matched by Yamina and Otzma's losses, and aggregate totals cannot say how much was new turnout. From 2021 to 2022 haredi lists grew 19% and right-wing lists 8%, while change-camp lists fell 0.8%, a pattern consistent with differential turnout but not proof of it. Model: 25,000 extra Netanyahu-bloc votes cut the chance of a change-led government by 1.3 points, more than ten times what a realistic field programme adds. Judgement: no triumphalism, no contempt for Likud, haredi, settler or Reservists-Economic voters, and no alarms about any community's turnout. Aim anger at decisions and leaders, never at groups of voters. Tell the bloc's own voters that turnout will be high, not that disaster looms.

principles.title: Four lists, one argument
principles.text: Evidence: across 111 studies, attacks only modestly lowered feelings toward the target and rarely won votes for the attacker. In a three-way Italian mayoral race, a challenger's attack on the incumbent hurt the attacker, and the candidate who stayed out gained 3.7 points. In 2022 Yesh Atid took about 18% of Meretz's 2021 voters, roughly nine times the votes by which Meretz then missed the threshold. Model: half a point of the vote moving from Yashar to the Democrats changes the chance of a change-led government by 0.01 points. The Democrats pass the threshold in about 99% of draws and Yisrael Beytenu in about 97%. Judgement: votes taken from an ally are worth almost nothing, and a public fight inside the bloc helps Likud. No paid or earned attacks between Yashar, Together, the Democrats and Yisrael Beytenu, and no 'vote for the biggest list' appeals that could drain an ally. Joint creative needs a written cost split approved by both lists' counsel and treasurers, because spending by linked bodies counts as party spending. No voter-level data passes between lists without written counsel clearance: the voter register is handed over on an undertaking never to pass it on.

principles.title: Test fast, inoculate early, spend late
principles.text: Evidence: in US campaigns' own experiments a single ad's effect was small on average, but ads routinely differed by about 50% from the average, and common theories of what persuades predicted poorly. The authors' simulations put 10-13% of a media budget into testing. Using pretests and machine learning to pick each person's message beat showing everyone the single best message by about 70% in US survey experiments on policy views, mostly on one of two issues, and targeting on more than one trait added nothing. Video added little persuasion over text. Ad persuasion fades fast: a half-life of about four days in a US presidential race and one to two days in smaller races, and about half the ad effect that survived to election day came from the final week. Warning voters of a coming attack and refuting it in advance builds resistance, but it decays after about two weeks (54-study meta-analysis). Wording tricks that worked in small studies failed at scale. Judgement: test 8-12 messages this week on 2,000-3,000 Jewish respondents with soft Netanyahu-bloc and traditional quotas. Inoculate against the predictable attacks now and refresh from Wed 21 Oct. Put most paid persuasion into 21-26 Oct.

principles.title: Threshold arithmetic, said with respect
principles.text: Evidence: in 2022 about 289,000 anti-Netanyahu votes were wasted when Meretz and Balad missed the threshold. Final polls misjudge lists near the line in both directions: lists averaging 3.5-4.5 seats in the final three weeks failed 22% of the time. Insurance voting for a small list depends on polls showing it near the line and on a clear coalition signal (experiments abroad). When a list withdraws, its voters scatter by their own views rather than follow their leader: after Zehut withdrew in 2019 in return for Netanyahu's promise, only about 29% of its voters went to Likud (ecological estimates). Model: Blue and White withdrawing and endorsing adds 1.7 points to the chance of a change-led government. Reservists-Economic withdrawing adds 1.6 points if 60% of its voters go to change lists but costs 1.0 point if most go right, and in both cases it raises Netanyahu's chance of 61. Judgement: rescue messaging is media, digital and calls to identified voters, timed around the final polls on Fri 23 Oct, not door work. Talk about arithmetic, never about people. No attacks on Gantz. Whether to address Reservists-Economic voters at all is a leadership decision. If they are addressed, describe the list as right-of-centre and reservist-led, and its voters as people who share the equal-burden cause.

issues.who_it_moves: Soft-right, traditional and centre-right Jewish voters. In IDI's Aug-Sep survey security was the first-ranked vote factor for 18% of Jews, in the top two for 39%, and in the top two for 47% on the right. Centre-right voters split on prime minister: Netanyahu 44%, Eisenkot 21%, Bennett 20% (JPPI, Sep). 61% were satisfied with the IDF's conduct of the war against 34% for the government, and 59% think an October 7-type attack could recur from Gaza (INSS, Sep). On 9 Oct, 48% trusted an Eisenkot-led government to fix the October 7 failures against 30% for Netanyahu (N12).
issues.frame: Evidence: an Israeli panel around October 7 found the threat built trust in the security forces, not in the government or the prime minister, whose standing tracked blame. A military biography raises perceived security competence whatever the party, but not warmth (US experiment). Reframing an issue and blaming the rival's record cut the rival's issue ownership by about 7 points on a 0-1 scale, while moving toward the rival's position did not help and once raised its ownership (Danish and US experiments). In the polarised US case the effect was larger among the attacker's own supporters, so the dent among Likud voters may be smaller. Competence messages beat ideological ones in an Italian field trial. In January 2015 a majority named cost of living and social issues their top concern while Netanyahu kept the security lead, and before the 2013 election he led on security while Labor led on the economy. He won both times. Judgement: compete on security, do not pivot away from it. Present it as preparation, competence and accountability: who saw the warnings, who failed, who will fix it. Praise the soldiers and question the government's decisions, never the reverse. Do not try to out-hawk Likud.
issues.owner: Yashar (Eisenkot) leads. Together (Bennett) and Yisrael Beytenu (Liberman) echo it in their own voices. The Democrats keep it to the base.
issues.risk: A security incident in the final days can pull the agenda toward Likud: a local terror attack within three months of an election has raised the right bloc's local share by about 1.35 points, and being in rocket range by 2-6 points. Credentials do not override identity, so the frame pays only where Eisenkot is close to Netanyahu on security, and no 2026 poll in our files asks who is best on security. Commission one this week. About three in ten Jews saw a recent strike in Syria as driven by election politics, but the bloc should never make that accusation itself. No uniforms or IDF framing, and written consent for any image of a soldier wounded or killed in service. The CEC has already removed Yashar and Bennett material over military imagery.

issues.issue: October 7 accountability and the state commission of inquiry
issues.who_it_moves: Soft Likud voters. In May, October 7 was the top reason (37%) 2022 Likud voters gave for considering a switch. On 9 Oct, 67% said the failures have not been fixed, including 40% of Netanyahu-bloc voters (N12). Support for a state commission among coalition voters was 37% in an N12 poll reported on 6 Oct and 52% in INSS's September survey, while only 27% of coalition voters said Netanyahu bears 'a great deal' of responsibility. 41% of all voters say October 7 does not affect their vote. The inquiry is decisive for 22% of secular 18-22-year-olds.
issues.frame: Evidence: in the same N12 poll more coalition voters backed a state commission (37%) than said Netanyahu bears a great deal of responsibility (27%), so an institutional question reaches further than personal blame. Fear and loss appeals reliably shift attitudes and intentions, more so with a clear action that removes the threat (meta-analysis of 127 papers, mostly outside politics). Attacks rarely win votes, but negative facts are memorable (111-study meta-analysis). Judgement: lead with repair and an independent state commission of inquiry, framed as what families, soldiers and border communities are owed. Pair the loss with the action: 'another four years without a commission, or a vote for a government that sets one up'. Do not ask Likud voters to blame their leader or regret their 2022 vote. Keep the personal-responsibility contrast for the base.
issues.owner: Yashar (Eisenkot) leads, with one joint commission pledge in the same words from all four lists. Bereaved and survivor families speak only on their own initiative and with written consent.
issues.risk: The issue has become partisan. Likud petitioned the CEC on 18 Sep against three Yashar videos on Netanyahu's conduct before October 7, alleging misleading editing, and no ruling had been reported. Every factual claim needs a sourced record and fair editing. Using the name or image of the fallen, the wounded or victims without written consent breaks the law and would backfire. Do not claim that Likud voters have changed their minds: the 2023 and 2026 polls asked different questions of different groups.

issues.who_it_moves: The widest cross-bloc wedge. 71.5% of Jews opposed the law freezing arrests of yeshiva students who do not report for service, and among religious groups only Haredim strongly backed it (IDI, Jul-Aug). In a December 2024 poll of 800 reservists who fought, 77% said exemptions are no longer affordable and 60% would consider not voting for a party that backs an exemption law, including 48% of right-wing reservists. The draft was the second reason (23%) 2022 Likud voters gave for considering a switch. It is in the top two issues for 34% of centrists and decisive for 26% of secular 18-22-year-olds. Shas has been losing working-class traditional voters over it.
issues.frame: Evidence: model: half a point of the vote moving from Shas and UTJ to the change lists adds 2.8 points to the chance of a change-led government. Threats to a group's standing make its strong identifiers angrier and more active (US). Appeals to an identity that rivals share reduced partisan hostility in a 25-treatment US megastudy. Arguments framed in the listener's own values persuaded more in US experiments (small online samples). Judgement: fairness to the families who serve, a shared burden for every citizen and a real path for yeshiva students to serve. Speak with respect for Torah study and in the language of tradition. 'Torah and service side by side: one burden for every family' is the kind of line to test. Reservists speak as civilians and parents, never in uniform. Present the draft as a policy test for any partner, not a ban on parties (see Coalition).
issues.owner: Together (Bennett) and Yisrael Beytenu (Liberman) carry the sharpest version. Yashar (Eisenkot) carries the fairness version to traditional voters. All four lists state the same policy.
issues.risk: Contempt for Haredim as a group would mobilise haredi voters. The CEC has enjoined a charity accused of paying Hasidim to stay home, and Degel HaTorah's spiritual leader called campaigns urging Haredim to abstain a 'great crime'. Lowering anyone's turnout is never an aim of this campaign. Keep the draft argument in secular and traditional channels, not in haredi media. A haredi party is one of the bloc's own routes to government (3.2% of outcomes in the formation model). For national-religious voters the draft is the top issue for only 15%. The equal-burden message depends on the reservist constituency, so speak respectfully of Reservists-Economic and its voters.

issues.who_it_moves: Right-wing Jews put cost of living first, and 43% of them say it makes no difference who you vote for (IDI Democracy Index 2025). It was the top concern of undecided voters (25%, Channel 12, July), the centre's lead issue (economy in the top two for 40.5%) and the second issue for 18-22-year-olds (25%). Among Jews it ties security as the first-ranked vote factor (18%). About 65% of Jews prefer a social-democratic economy. The polls fold housing into cost of living, so there is no separate evidence on housing.
issues.frame: Evidence: in January 2015, 53% named cost of living and social issues their top concern, but ownership was split across several parties while Netanyahu held the security lead, and he won. Issue ownership moves most on issues no party owns (Belgian experiment). Economic views do not line up with Israeli left and right. Information-rich messages persuade more than thin ones (US). Judgement: one costed household plan for the whole bloc, on housing, prices and commuting time. Sell it as competence, 'who can actually deliver', not ideology. Link it to the draft: who works, who serves and who pays.
issues.owner: All four lists, one shared plan. Yashar leads it for Route 4 commuters and Yisrael Beytenu in Russian-speaking cities.
issues.risk: Four lists with four plans split ownership, which is what happened in 2015. Economic messages do not move bloc identity by themselves, so pair the plan with security credibility. Low efficacy on the right means the message must say what will change, not only what is wrong. Promise only what is in published platforms.

issues.who_it_moves: The base and secular voters, including secular Likud voters. Religion and state is the first-ranked vote factor for 13% of Jews and the left's top issue (39% in the top two). About two in three Jews support civil marriage, 64.8% opposed the gender-segregation law, and at least 35% of Likud voters take the opposite side to their religious partners on religion in public life. Secular voters are about a third of Likud's electorate. 50-60% of Russian speakers are secular.
issues.frame: Evidence: coded religious language reached religious voters without costing support among others in one US experiment (low confidence). Appeals to shared identity reduced partisan hostility (US). Israeli voters choose parties whose national story matches their own. Judgement: a shared Jewish public space every Israeli can live in: civil marriage, no gender segregation in public services, fair rules for all. Speak from tradition, not against religion. Lead with it for the base and for secular Russian speakers. With traditional voters, keep it inside the fairness and draft argument.
issues.owner: Yisrael Beytenu and Together lead. The Democrats carry it to the base. Yashar uses the tradition-friendly version.
issues.risk: If it sounds like hostility to religion it costs traditional and national-religious voters and hands haredi and religious-Zionist leaders a threat to rally against. It is not a lead message for soft Likud voters.

issues.who_it_moves: Mainly the base. Judicial reform is the first-ranked vote factor for only 6% of Jews (18% in the top two). In January 2025, 8.5% named the overhaul the government's top priority, though 55% opposed it. 40% of right-wing Jews said it was not the time, and 30% agreed it concentrates too much power. A small right-wing majority backed the attorney-general law in July. Undecided voters name polarisation as a top concern (15%), and unity is the centre's top issue (30%).
issues.frame: Evidence: support for the 2023 judicial overhaul tracked attachment to Netanyahu and hostility to partisan opponents (Israeli panel, 2023). Campaign attention to an issue often teaches partisans their own side's line rather than changing what they weigh (US panel data). In Israel, salient electoral competition raised partisan hostility, and priming cooperation between parties raised tolerance in a survey experiment. Judgement: for the base, democracy and the rule of law. For everyone else, honest and competent government and national unity, not court powers. Do not lead with the overhaul outside the base.
issues.owner: The Democrats and Together carry it to the base. Yashar and Yisrael Beytenu use the governance and unity version.
issues.risk: Leading with it turns the vote into a referendum on Netanyahu's camp and activates the attachment that drove support for the overhaul. A tribal showdown raises turnout on both sides, and Likud is already working to bring out supporters in its low-turnout strongholds.

issues.issue: Coalition with Arab parties: inoculating against Likud's wedge
issues.who_it_moves: This is Likud's best wedge with the bloc's persuasion targets. 61% of Jews opposed including Ra'am in the next government (IDI, July), and 59% opposed an Arab party in the coalition while 53% supported a haredi party (Maariv, 7-8 Oct). In December 2025, 57.8% of Jews would not support a government relying on Ra'am, while about a third would under some condition. Model: the change lists alone reach 61 in 6.9% of forecast draws, and in about 26% with Ra'am.
issues.frame: Evidence: warning voters of a coming attack and refuting it in advance gives more resistance than supportive messages, and the effect decays after about two weeks (54-study meta-analysis). The CEC has twice ordered fakes of this kind removed: a Likud image of Bennett and Lapid joining hands with Arab party leaders (February) and an RZP AI video of an Eisenkot lookalike with Mahmoud Abbas and Mansour Abbas (July). Repeating a rumour raises belief in it, and a correction from an unexpected same-side source worked best among attentive respondents (US). Uncertainty about a party's coalition prospects costs it votes (studies in seven countries). Judgement: inoculate now and again from Wed 21 Oct, about the fakery, not about Arab politicians: 'Expect AI fakes in the final days. The election committee has already ordered two removed. Here is who will lead a change government, and on what terms.' Use only the conditional line on the Coalition page: the change bloc leads, any outside support is public, in writing and on a published programme, and security policy is not traded. Bennett, Liberman and Eisenkot deliver it. Beyond the prebunk and the agreed line, do not lead paid content with the subject, and never repeat a fake's claim in a headline.
issues.owner: Bloc leadership jointly: one agreed line, in the same words, from all four lists. The exact wording is a leadership decision.
issues.risk: An absolute pledge would confine the bloc to its smallest route to 61 and invite a broken promise, and voters punish parties they see as compromising: Blue and White fell from 33 seats to 8 after Gantz joined Netanyahu in 2020. Language that treats Arab citizens or their votes as illegitimate is wrong and can backfire. After Likud's 2019 camera campaign Arab-list votes rose 39.5%, and the Task Force on Arab Citizens warns that framing reliance on Arab parties as illegitimate deepens alienation. In a 2019 survey experiment, centre-left ads on equality aimed at Arab citizens did not cost support among Jewish voters (one advocacy-linked study, low weight). Never answer the wedge by attacking Arab citizens or their parties.

issues.issue: The north and the Gaza-envelope communities
issues.who_it_moves: Northern Jewish towns, returning residents, and voters elsewhere who identify with them. In April, 65% of Haifa and Northern District residents said the state is abandoning the north and 70% gave the government a poor grade, including 31% of coalition voters. Vote intention there was opposition 38%, coalition 26%, undecided 27% (Midgam, n=505, margin 5.7 points). Kiryat Shmona's Likud share fell from 58% (2020) to 49% (2022). Reports on returns conflict: AFP put fewer than half of Kiryat Shmona's residents at home in April, ynet said about 40% had returned in August, and the Christian Science Monitor said almost 40% had not returned by September. Returnees skew older and poorer. In the Gaza envelope about 90% of evacuees had returned by September 2025, with newcomers mostly in Sderot, while the hardest-hit kibbutzim remain largely displaced. INSS found confidence in IDF readiness at 49% for the north. The atlas flags 49 localities within 5 km of Lebanon and 40 within 7 km of Gaza as displaced.
issues.frame: Evidence: Israeli men old enough to serve in the mismanaged 1973 war turned durably against the party that ran it, with no such effect after well-managed wars. But rocket range and actual hits have raised the right's local vote, and a panel study (seminar abstract only) finds persistent rightward shifts since October 7. In development towns, political identity is local and tied to place (qualitative study). Judgement: local and practical. Rebuilding, schools, jobs, health services and a secure border, with accountability for the abandonment, delivered by local people who lived it. In Likud-leaning northern towns this is persuasion, not turnout work.
issues.owner: Yashar (Eisenkot has met would-be Shas defectors in Kiryat Shmona and Shlomi), Yisrael Beytenu in Russian-speaking northern cities, and local leaders of all four lists.
issues.risk: Exploiting trauma, or using images of victims without written consent. Displaced residents vote at their registered station unless special stations are set for evacuees, as 83 were in the delayed February 2025 northern municipal elections. Confirm the 2026 arrangements with the CEC and counsel before telling anyone where to vote, and give them practical information, including free intercity buses and trains from 20:00 on Mon 26 Oct. The bloc does not organise rides. Generic turnout pushes in Likud-leaning towns help Likud, which is targeting its own low-turnout strongholds.

audiences.size_note: Yashar puts the soft-Likud pool at about 200,000 voters, a pool rather than an expected gain. In May only 58% of 2022 Likud voters were sure to vote Likud again. About 0.6% of all voters are torn between the blocs (N12, 9 Oct). Traditional voters gave 66.5% of their votes to the coalition parties in 2022. Model: half a point of the vote (about 24,000) moving from Likud to the change lists adds 3.1 points to the chance of a change-led government.
audiences.what_moves: October 7 (37% of wavering 2022 Likud voters) and the draft (23%), then Netanyahu's conduct (14%) and division (13%). Right-wing Jews put cost of living first. At least 35% of Likud voters disagree with their religious partners on religion in public life and court powers. Among traditional voters Likud's share rose from 39% to 46.5% between 2021 and 2022, so this group moves. A critique framed as loyalty left US conservatives' stated likelihood of voting for Trump about 19 points lower on a 0-100 scale than the same critique framed as fairness (small online sample, no no-message control).
audiences.message: You can stay who you are and vote for change. A government led by people who served will fix what failed on October 7, share the burden fairly and bring down the cost of living. Loyalty to the country and to those who serve comes first.
audiences.messenger: Eisenkot, Bennett and Liberman. Former Likud voters and local traditional figures in their own towns. Former security chiefs speaking as civilians about specific decisions.
audiences.channel: Earned coverage on Channel 12, N12 and ynet. Tested paid video from Wed 21 Oct. Forwards from family and friends on WhatsApp. Persuasion calls to identified soft voters in the Persuasion battleground and Supporter-list ground towns (see Field).
audiences.avoid: Blaming them for their 2022 vote. Mocking Likud voters or traditional and Mizrahi identity. Leading with the judicial overhaul. Golan or Lapid as messengers to this group. Anything that makes Arab-party partnership the topic. Any message meant to keep them home: the aim is their vote, never their abstention.

audiences.size_note: Shas fell from 11 seats in 2022 to about 7 in several polls, losing tens of thousands of working-class traditional voters to Otzma, Likud and Yashar, and a Shas activist put its hard base at about 4 seats. The 13 Oct forecast has Shas at 9. Traditional-religious voters gave Likud 47%, RZP-Otzma 17% and Shas 10% in 2022. Model: half a point of the vote moving from Shas and UTJ to the change lists adds 2.8 points to the chance of a change-led government.
audiences.what_moves: The draft crisis, prices and respect. Shas and Otzma are fighting over the same traditional voters, and 15% of Otzma's current voters voted Shas in 2022. Shas has collapsed among 18-22-year-olds. In development towns political identity is local and tied to place (qualitative study). Coded religious language may reach religious voters without costing others (one US experiment, low confidence).
audiences.message: Torah and service are both Jewish values. A fair share of the burden, respect for tradition and lower living costs for working families, from a government that keeps its promises to the periphery.
audiences.messenger: Eisenkot in person (he has met would-be Shas defectors in Kiryat Shmona, Shlomi and Or Yehuda), traditional local figures, and rabbis who choose to speak. Not secular-liberal national leaders.
audiences.channel: House meetings in private homes, with no gifts or catering beyond what election counsel clears. Local WhatsApp groups, local news and the bloc's allocated radio slots.
audiences.avoid: Contempt for Haredim, rabbis or Shas voters. Secular-versus-religious framing. Taking the draft argument into haredi media. Anything that could read as discouraging haredi voting: lowering anyone's turnout is never an aim, and the CEC has enjoined a group accused of paying Hasidim to stay home.

audiences.size_note: About 15% of the population (about 900,000 people), worth 16-17 seats at full turnout, and Likud has drawn about 3-4 seats from them. The atlas's Russian-speaking towns segment has about 580,000 eligible voters in 10 localities, with 2022 turnout of 59% and a 2026 projection of 40% change lists and 56% Netanyahu bloc. Yisrael Beytenu has mapped the polling stations where Likud did best among Russian speakers.
audiences.what_moves: Generations differ. Adults who immigrated in the 1990s sit to the right of native-born Israelis, those who arrived as teenagers lean centrist, and the Israeli-born second generation votes like other native-born Israelis. 50-60% are secular. FSU immigrants reported more abstention than other Jews in 2013 surveys. No 2026 Russian-language message poll was found, so the message here is judgement: security competence, freedom from religious coercion and an equal burden are the natural ground.
audiences.message: Security run by professionals, freedom from religious coercion (civil marriage and fair rules for all), an equal burden in the army and lower living costs. Respect for the immigrants who built and defend the country.
audiences.messenger: Liberman and Yisrael Beytenu's Russian-speaking candidates first, then Russian-speaking figures in Yashar and Together. Second-generation Israelis talking to their parents.
audiences.channel: Channel 9, Russian-language news sites, Facebook and Russian-language Telegram channels, family WhatsApp groups, and a Russian-language how-to-vote card. In 2022 invalid ballots ran at 0.80% in Russian-speaking-segment localities against 0.35% in liberal cities (a locality-level pattern, not proof about individuals).
audiences.avoid: Treating Russian speakers as one bloc. Soviet or 'Russians' stereotypes. Talking down to older immigrants. Hebrew-only creative. Change lists competing for the same voters where Yisrael Beytenu leads.

audiences.size_note: About 550,000 first-time voters, roughly 10-12 seats (Midgam for N12). Among Jewish first-time voters Yashar had 16% and Likud 14%, with 10% undecided. 74% place themselves right or centre-right, Netanyahu led Eisenkot 47-37, and 21% expect to vote differently from their parents. Among 18-22-year-olds 67% were certain to vote (Jews 71%), and 14% were undecided on a party (young women 20%).
audiences.what_moves: Security (27%) and cost of living (25%) lead. The draft is decisive for 26% of secular youth against 6% of religious youth, and the October 7 inquiry for 22% against 5%. Among secular 18-22-year-olds Together had 20%, Yashar 18% and the Democrats 17%. Young Jewish adults are the most right-wing age group (73-75% of 18-34s in 2022). Friend-to-friend texting raised turnout about 2-3 points among those assigned and about 8-12 points among those actually messaged (US, 2018). At 18-22, 90% use Instagram, 80% TikTok and 77% Telegram.
audiences.message: Housing you can afford, a fair share of the burden for those who serve, and an honest inquiry into what went wrong. Your first vote helps decide this. Most people your age are voting.
audiences.messenger: Friends and classmates, young reservists and students speaking as civilians, the lists' young candidates, and creators who disclose any payment.
audiences.channel: Instagram, TikTok and Telegram, friend-to-friend messages and campus activity. Practical facts: vote at the polling station of your registered address, intercity buses and trains are free from 20:00 on Mon 26 Oct, and soldiers vote by double envelope.
audiences.avoid: Reaching soldiers or reservists through IDF units, bases, commanders or employers. Uniforms and IDF framing. Children under 15 in any material. Saying the race is lost or that one vote does not matter. Change lists fighting each other over secular youth.

audiences.size_note: In a Dialog poll of national-religious voters (31 Aug-2 Sep), RZP-Zehut had about 30%, Likud 17%, Otzma 12%, Amcha 6%, Yashar 4% and Together 3%, with 13% undecided. Yashar estimates it already has 1-1.5 seats from religious Zionists and aims for about two more from traditional and moderate religious-Zionist voters. The atlas projects 22% for the change lists in religious-Zionist towns inside the Green Line and 14% in national-religious West Bank settlements.
audiences.what_moves: Security (35%) and Jewish identity (25%) lead. The draft is the top issue for only 15% and settlement for 14%. The national-religious public moved right between 2019 and 2022, and its preference for a full-right coalition rose from 61% to 85%, though moderates may drift to non-sectoral parties. Among religious reservists who fought, 35% would consider not voting for a party that backs a draft exemption. No data was found on which media reach this group.
audiences.message: Jewish identity and responsible statecraft together. Security led by people who served, Torah and service side by side, and a government that treats the religious-Zionist community as a partner, not an opponent.
audiences.messenger: Matan Kahana and religious-Zionist candidates on the change lists, Bennett, and educators, rabbis and religious reservists who choose to speak, as civilians.
audiences.channel: Yashar's dedicated headquarters for Gush Etzion, Efrat, Givat Shmuel and Ariel, community WhatsApp groups and house meetings.
audiences.avoid: Attacks on settlers or settlements. Mocking religious life. Leading with the judicial overhaul or civil marriage. Making Arab-party partnership the topic. Expecting large yields in national-religious settlements.

audiences.size_note: The atlas's secular-liberal urban segment has about 1.4 million eligible voters, projected at 64% for the change lists, with 2022 turnout of 67%. Opposition supporters are more certain to vote than coalition supporters (80% against 72% in July, 86% against 81% on 7-8 Oct). An N12 analysis puts the bloc's target at above 76% turnout among its supporters in the Sharon, Tel Aviv and Haifa. Model: 25,000 extra change-list votes add 1.7 points to the chance of a change-led government, and 50,000 add 3.4.
audiences.what_moves: Messages saying turnout will be high beat messages lamenting low turnout, mainly among occasional voters (US). Telling individuals the race is close moved turnout by at most about 0.8 points (US).
